# Hypertrophy: KiteSink fitness field guide

Training for muscle size. Each entry gives the point, the reasoning, what to do, how well supported it is, and its sources.

## Guidance

### More weekly sets build more muscle, with diminishing returns

**Muscle growth rises with weekly hard sets per muscle, but each added set gives less than the one before it.**

A meta-regression of 67 studies and 2,058 participants (79% men, average age about 25) found that gains in muscle size rose as weekly set volume rose, with diminishing returns. Strength gains levelled off much sooner. The model gave a set that only trains a muscle as a helper half the credit of a direct set.

- Add sets slowly, and only when progress at your current number has stalled.

Volume · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w)

### 12 to 20 weekly sets per muscle is a reasonable range for trained lifters

**A review of trained young men found 12-20 sets per muscle per week a sensible target. Treat it as a guide, not a cap.**

A systematic review of seven trials in men with at least a year of lifting compared under 12, 12-20 and over 20 weekly sets (six trials were pooled). Moderate and high volumes did not differ for the quadriceps or biceps. High volume did better for the triceps. The newer 67-study analysis found diminishing returns but no clear ceiling, so 20 is not a hard limit.

- If you train a muscle fewer than 12 sets a week and progress is slow, test a small increase.

Volume · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Baz-Valle 2022](https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2022-0017), [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w)

### Almost any structured programme beats no training, and multiple sets rank highest for size

**In a network meta-analysis, every prescription beat no exercise, and multi-set programmes ranked highest for hypertrophy.**

The hypertrophy network pooled 119 trials and 3,364 healthy adults. All 12 prescriptions beat non-exercise controls and promoted size comparably. The highest-ranked for hypertrophy was higher-load, multiple-set, twice-weekly training. Rankings are not proof that the top option is better than the rest.

- Choose a plan you can follow for months, with more than one set per exercise.

Volume · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Currier 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106807)

### Sets ended closer to failure tended to build more muscle

**In a meta-regression, hypertrophy improved as sets ended nearer to failure, while strength gains were similar across a wide range.**

The analysis estimated reps in reserve (RIR, the reps left before failure) for each study from its description, so the exact shape of the curve is unclear, as the authors state. Muscle size had a clear negative slope with RIR. For strength, the intervals included zero, meaning no clear relationship.

- End most hard sets with only a few reps left in reserve.

Effort · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Robinson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02069-2)

### Going to absolute failure has not shown a clear edge over stopping just short

**Training to momentary failure was not clearly better for muscle than stopping close to it.**

A meta-analysis of 15 studies found no advantage for momentary failure (effect size 0.12, interval -0.13 to 0.37). In a trial of 18 trained people over 8 weeks, legs trained to failure or to about 1-2 reps in reserve grew the same. A 13-study review found no hypertrophy difference when volume was equal.

- Use 1-2 reps in reserve on most sets, and save true failure for safe exercises such as machines.

Effort · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Refalo 2023](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01784-y), [Refalo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2024.2321021), [Vieira 2021](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000003936)

### Reps in reserve is a useful guide, but most lifters misjudge it

**RIR tracks how hard a set was, but people tend to underpredict how many reps they have left, by about one rep on average.**

In 29 squatters, an RIR-based effort rating moved in step with bar speed. A scoping review and meta-analysis of 12 studies and 414 people found lifters underpredicted reps to failure by 0.95 reps on average, with wide variation. Guesses were better close to the end of a set and on sets of 12 reps or fewer. Training experience did not clearly change accuracy in the pooled data, though one study of 141 people saw a tendency to improve with experience.

- Rate RIR on sets of about 12 reps or fewer.
- Occasionally check yourself with one set to failure on a safe exercise.

Effort · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Zourdos 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001049), [Halperin 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01559-x), [Pelland 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01667-2), [Steele 2017](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.4105)

### The effective-reps idea is a useful rule of thumb, not a measured law

**The idea that only the last few reps near failure drive growth fits the direction of the data. No fixed cut-off has been shown.**

Effective (or stimulating) reps is a coaching model. It matches the finding that sets nearer failure tend to build more size. The meta-regression showed a gradual slope with estimated RIR, not a cliff, and its authors note the RIR estimates are rough. The reviews of RIR methods find they differ in accuracy, so a hard rule such as "the last five reps" is not supported.

- Use the idea to remind yourself to make sets hard, not to count reps.

Effort · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Robinson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02069-2), [Pelland 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01667-2), [Halperin 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01559-x)

### Where the effective-reps model stops working

**The model assumes a rep near failure is worth the same at any load and that you can tell which reps those are. Both are shaky.**

It also leaves out exercise choice, muscle length and fatigue across sets. A trial that took sets to failure with heavier and lighter loads found similar fibre glycogen depletion in both fibre types, which fits with load mattering less at failure. Sets that stopped about 1-2 reps short still grew muscle as well as failure sets, and RIR is hard to judge exactly.

- Treat the model as a teaching tool and judge your plan by results over months.

Effort · Advanced · Thin evidence · Sources: [Morton 2019](https://doi.org/10.1113/jp278056), [Refalo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2024.2321021), [Halperin 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01559-x)

### Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are hard

**Muscle growth was similar with light and heavy loads when sets were taken close to failure.**

A meta-analysis of 45 studies found similar hypertrophy for loads above and at or below 60% of one-rep max (1RM). Another of 28 studies (747 adults), using sets to volitional failure, agreed. In 49 resistance-trained men over 12 weeks, 20-25 reps at about 30-50% 1RM grew muscle as much as 8-12 reps at 75-90%.

- Pick a load you can control through the full range and take the set close to failure.

Load and reps · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Refalo 2021](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2021.1898094), [Lopez 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002585), [Morton 2016](https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00154.2016)

### Heavier loads give better strength gains

**If one-rep-max strength matters to you, train with heavier loads at least part of the time.**

The network meta-analysis found loads above 80% of 1RM maximised strength gains. Pooled results of sets to failure showed high-load training beat low-load for strength. A separate analysis found higher loads improved 1RM strength, with an effect size of 0.34. Muscle size did not follow the same pattern.

- Include some sets in the 5-8 rep range if you also want a stronger one-rep max.

Load and reps · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Currier 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106807), [Lopez 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002585), [Refalo 2021](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2021.1898094)

### Adding reps and adding weight both work as progression

**In new lifters, progressing by reps or by load gave the same strength and muscle gains over 10 weeks.**

Thirty-nine previously untrained people (20 men, 19 women) had one leg progress by load and the other by reps. Leg extension 1RM and thigh muscle area rose by similar amounts in both. This was a short trial in beginners, so it may not transfer to advanced lifters.

- Add reps within a range first, then raise the load and drop back to the low end of the range.

Programming · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [Chaves 2024](https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2256-5857)

### With weekly sets matched, training a muscle more often adds little growth

**Once total weekly sets are equal, how often you train a muscle makes little difference to size.**

The meta-regression found the effect of frequency on hypertrophy compatible with a negligible effect. In 21 people given the same weekly volume over 9 weeks, two sessions a week and four sessions a week gave the same muscle and strength gains. In 24 men, training one or three times a week gave similar thigh results.

- Pick the number of weekly sessions you can keep, then spread your sets across them.

Frequency and splits · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w), [Hamarsland 2022](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2021.789403), [Neves 2022](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0276154)

### Full-body and split routines give similar results

**A meta-analysis found no meaningful difference in strength or muscle size between split and full-body routines.**

Fourteen studies with 392 participants compared the two. Gains in bench press and leg strength, arm and thigh muscle area and lean mass were similar. The review could not say what happens when volume differs, so choose the layout by schedule and preference.

- Choose the split that fits your week and that you enjoy.

Frequency and splits · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Ramos-Campo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000004774)

### Use a full range of motion by default; lengthened partials also work

**Full range of motion is the safe default. Partial reps done in the stretched half held up well in newer trials.**

A meta-analysis of 16 studies found full range beat partial range for lower-limb muscle growth (effect size 0.88) and strength. No clear difference appeared in muscle thickness overall. A 12-week trial across 15 sites (163 and 134 people in the two arms) found lengthened-partial and full-range training practically equivalent for arm and thigh size, and an 8-week trial in 13 trained people agreed.

- Move through the full range you can control, and keep partial reps for the stretched end.

Exercises and rest · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Pallarés 2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14006), [Gschneidner 2025](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2025.2567805), [Havers 2025](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsc.70087)

### Loading a muscle in its stretched position grew more in several trials

**Exercises that load a muscle when it is long gave bigger gains than versions that load it short, in trials that compared them.**

Seated leg curls grew the whole hamstrings more than prone leg curls (+14% against +9%, 20 adults, 12 weeks). Overhead cable triceps extensions beat neutral-arm ones (+19.9% against +13.9%, 21 adults, 12 weeks). In 42 young women, calf raises done in the lower, stretched half grew the medial calf more than full or top-half range.

- Include one exercise per muscle that loads it stretched, such as seated leg curls or overhead triceps extensions.

Exercises and rest · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Maeo 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002523), [Maeo 2023](https://doi.org/10.1080/17461391.2022.2100279), [Kassiano 2023](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000004460)

### Rest long enough to repeat your reps; 2 to 5 minutes gave similar growth in trained men

**Longer rest keeps reps up across sets. In trained men, resting 2 or 5 minutes gave similar muscle gains.**

A review of 35 studies found 3-5 minutes rest allowed more reps over several sets. In 13 strength-trained men, 2 and 5 minute rests gave similar muscle and strength gains over two 3-month blocks. A bench press needed 3-5 minutes to hold reps, a single-joint exercise about 2. In 12 untrained men, 2.5 minutes beat 1 minute for arm size.

- Rest about 3 minutes between heavy compound sets and about 2 minutes between isolation sets.

Exercises and rest · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [de Salles 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/11315230-000000000-00000), [Ahtiainen 2005](https://doi.org/10.1519/15604.1), [Senna 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001142), [Buresh 2009](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e318185f14a)

### Lift under control; very slow reps are not needed

**Controlled reps work. Reps of 10 seconds or more are best avoided, and slowing the lowering phase had no clear extra effect on size.**

An umbrella review of 14 meta-analyses suggested avoiding very slow reps of 10 seconds or more. A meta-analysis of nine studies found uncertain effects of slower lowering on hypertrophy. A review of six studies in 119 untrained people was mixed, and a tempo review notes the evidence is not clear-cut.

- Lower the weight in about 2 seconds and lift without bouncing.

Exercises and rest · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Bernárdez-Vázquez 2022](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2022.949021), [Amdi 2025](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2025.2535198), [Hackett 2018](https://doi.org/10.1080/17461391.2018.1434563), [Wilk 2021](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01465-2)

### Drop sets match straight sets for growth and can save time

**Drop sets built about the same muscle as normal sets in a pooled analysis, so the case for them is time and variety.**

A meta-analysis of six studies (142 adults) found both drop sets and normal sets increased muscle size, with no significant difference between them. A systematic review of advanced techniques also lists drop sets as a time-saving tool but says evidence is too thin for firm dosing guidance.

- Add one drop set at the end of an isolation exercise when you are short on time.

Special techniques · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Sødal 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00620-5), [Krzysztofik 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16244897)

### Supersets let you do the same work in less time

**Supersets gave similar volume and similar strength and size results in shorter sessions.**

A meta-analysis of 19 studies with 313 people compared supersets with straight sets. Total reps and volume load were similar and sessions were shorter. Supersets felt harder and raised markers of exertion. Pairing opposing muscles kept volume up better than pairing the same muscle.

- Pair opposing muscles, such as chest and back, when you are short on time.

Special techniques · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Zhang 2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02176-8)

### Rest-pause and cluster sets are fatigue and time tools, not growth boosters

**Pooled reviews found cluster sets and similar set structures give about the same size and strength as straight sets.**

A review of 17 studies found no set structure beat another for strength or hypertrophy, and a review of 29 studies found cluster sets matched traditional sets, possibly with less fatigue. One trial in 18 trained people found rest-pause grew thigh thickness more but not other sites.

- Use cluster or rest-pause sets when you want heavy reps with less fatigue, not as a growth hack.

Special techniques · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Prestes 2019](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001923), [Jukic 2021](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01423-4), [Davies 2021](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01408-3)

### Blood-flow restriction can build size with light loads, but needs care

**Light loads with a cuff that restricts blood flow built muscle similarly to heavy training, but built less strength.**

A meta-analysis found similar hypertrophy for high-load training and low-load training with blood-flow restriction (BFR), while strength favoured high load. A position stand sets out methods and safety for practitioners. Cuff width and pressure matter, and people with vascular or clotting conditions should involve a clinician first.

- Learn cuff width and pressure from a qualified practitioner, and ask a clinician if you have a vascular condition.

Special techniques · Advanced · Some support · Sources: [Lixandrão 2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0795-y), [Patterson 2019](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2019.00533)

### Put the exercises that matter most first

**Reps and volume are higher for an exercise placed early in a session, and pre-exhaustion gave no extra benefit.**

A review of exercise order found total repetitions were higher when an exercise was done at the start of a session. A 12-week trial in 39 trained people found pre-exhaustion (isolation before compound) gave no greater benefit than putting compound exercises first.

- Start with the lifts and muscles you most want to improve.

Programming · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Simão 2012](https://doi.org/10.2165/11597240-000000000-00000), [Fisher 2014](https://doi.org/10.1139/apnm-2014-0162)

### Warm up with lighter sets of the first lift; save long stretches for later

**Warming up helps performance. Long static stretches right before lifting can reduce it slightly.**

A meta-analysis of 32 studies found warm-ups improved performance in 79% of measured outcomes. A review found static stretches of 60 seconds or more per muscle lowered performance by 4.6%, against 1.1% for shorter holds, when tested right afterwards. A squat trial found extra heavy or fast warm-up sets gave no clear gain in total reps or volume.

- Do two or three lighter, increasing sets of your first lift before working sets.
- Hold long stretches for after training.

Programming · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Fradkin 2010](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e3181c643a0), [Behm 2016](https://doi.org/10.1139/apnm-2015-0235), [Souza 2024](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.17347)

### Deloads are common practice, but trials do not yet show they are needed

**Coaches use deloads regularly. The one small trial in beginners found cutting volume in weeks 4 and 8 neither helped nor hurt.**

A deload is a period of reduced training stress, defined by consensus among 21 coaches who finished a Delphi study. In 246 strength and physique athletes, deloads came about every 5.6 weeks and lasted about 6.4 days. In 19 untrained men, deload weeks did not change muscle growth over 8 weeks. Experienced lifters were not tested.

- Plan a lighter week about every five or six weeks, or sooner when performance drops for several sessions or joints ache.

Programming · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Bell 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00633-0), [Rogerson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00691-y), [Pancar 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-40612-5)

### Periodising your training helps strength more than muscle size

**When volume was equal, planned changes in volume and load helped strength but not muscle size.**

A meta-analysis of 35 studies found periodised training had a small advantage for 1RM strength over non-periodised training. Hypertrophy did not differ between periodised and non-periodised, or between linear and undulating, plans. Undulating beat linear plans for 1RM only in trained people.

- Vary rep ranges across the week if it keeps training interesting, but do not expect it to change size.

Programming · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Moesgaard 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01636-1)

### Muscle size gains in the first weeks partly reflect swelling

**Measured size rises in the first weeks, but some of that early gain is swelling from training stress, not new muscle tissue.**

In 25 sedentary men, thigh muscle area rose 9.6% over 8 weeks, and the authors judged real hypertrophy likely appeared around weeks 3-4. Other researchers found early increases came with swelling markers, and a review argues true hypertrophy appears after roughly 18 sessions. The timing is debated.

- Judge progress over months, not the first three weeks.

Programming · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [DeFreitas 2011](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-011-1905-4), [Damas 2016](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-015-3243-4), [Damas 2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-017-3792-9)

### How to read a training study before you act on it

**Check who was studied, for how long, how muscle was measured and how failure was defined before copying a result.**

Most volume and frequency data come from short trials in young people: in the 67-study set, the average age was about 25 and 79% were men. Studies also define failure differently and often do not report reps in reserve. A single trial is weak evidence next to a meta-analysis, and an interval that includes zero means no clear difference.

- Ask who was studied and for how many weeks before applying a finding.

Programming · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w), [Pelland 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01667-2)

### Short sleep lowers lifting performance

**Sleep loss lowered exercise performance in a large meta-analysis, and one small study found lower muscle protein synthesis after a sleepless night.**

A meta-analysis of 69 publications defined sleep loss as 6 hours or less in 24 and found an average 7.56% drop in performance. A review of 17 studies found restricted sleep reduced force on compound lifts. In 13 adults, one night without sleep cut muscle protein synthesis by 18%. Long-term growth effects were not tested.

- Protect regular, full nights of sleep, especially before heavy sessions.

Recovery · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Craven 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y), [Knowles 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2018.01.012), [Lamon 2021](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.14660)

## Common mistakes

### Judging a session by how sore you are

**Soreness does not show that a session worked, and its absence does not show that it failed.**

A review found muscle damage is not what drives hypertrophy, and protocols causing little damage still grow muscle. Soreness is largest early on and fades as you adapt. Chasing it can lead to piling on volume or exercises you cannot recover from.

- Judge sessions by reps, load and effort recorded in a log.

Recovery · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Damas 2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-017-3792-9)

### Repeating the same weights and reps with no log

**Without a record, you cannot tell whether you are adding reps or load, which is what progression means.**

In 39 beginners, adding load and adding reps each raised strength and thigh muscle area over 10 weeks. Both methods need you to know last week's numbers. Writing down weight, reps and effort for each set takes little time and makes stalls easy to spot.

- Log weight, reps and reps in reserve for every working set.

Programming · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [Chaves 2024](https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2256-5857)

### Cutting the range of motion to lift heavier

**Shortening the rep to add weight tended to give up size in the lower body. Partials in the stretched half are different.**

A meta-analysis of 16 studies found full range gave larger lower-limb muscle gains than partial range. Lengthened partials, done on purpose in the stretched half with control, matched full range in a large 12-week trial. Half reps that skip the stretched part, done only to move more weight, are the mistake.

- Lower under control to the stretched position and drive up without bouncing.

Exercises and rest · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Pallarés 2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14006), [Gschneidner 2025](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2025.2567805)

### Ending every set far from failure

**Sets that stop well short of failure leave growth on the table, and self-chosen loads are often light.**

The meta-regression found muscle size improved as sets ended closer to failure. People who choose their own weights average about 53% of 1RM. Sets that stop when the work first feels uncomfortable can sit many reps from failure. Many beginners find it hard to judge how many reps remain.

- Raise the load or reps until the last rep of each working set looks slow and hard.

Effort · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Robinson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02069-2), [Steele 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01717-9)

### Jumping to very high volume straight away

**More sets add less each time, so a big jump from your current volume mostly adds fatigue.**

The dose-response analysis shows diminishing returns on weekly sets. A small trial of 16 trained people found a volume built from each person's own logs beat a fixed 22 weekly sets. Coaches therefore add sets in small steps and watch whether performance holds.

- Add 1-3 sets per muscle per week, then check performance for two weeks.

Volume · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w), [Scarpelli 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000003558)

### Cutting rest so short that your reps fall

**Very short rests lower the reps you can do on later sets, and with it the total work.**

In a trial, a 1-minute rest gave fewer total reps over five sets than 3-5 minutes on a bench press. A review of 35 studies found 3-5 minutes allowed more reps over several sets. Short rests are fine for small isolation moves, but for compound lifts they cost volume.

- Rest long enough to repeat most of your first set's reps.

Exercises and rest · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Senna 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001142), [de Salles 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/11315230-000000000-00000)

## Key numbers

| Number | What it is | Support | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12-20 sets per muscle per week | Weekly sets per muscle: A range from a review of trained young men; a newer analysis found no clear ceiling. | Some support | [Baz-Valle 2022](https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2022-0017) |
| 0.95 reps, average miss | Average underprediction of reps to failure: Across 12 studies, lifters guessed they had about one rep fewer in the tank than they did. | Some support | [Halperin 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01559-x) |
| 53 % of 1RM, average | Load people choose when left alone: Average self-selected load across exercises in a scoping review; light unless sets end near failure. | Thin evidence | [Steele 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01717-9) |
| 80+ % of 1RM | Load that maximised strength gains: Loads above this ranked best for strength in a network meta-analysis. All loads comparably built muscle. | Well supported | [Currier 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106807) |
| 60 or less % of 1RM | Upper limit of light-load training in a meta-analysis: Training at or below this load built muscle similarly to heavier loads, but built less strength. | Well supported | [Refalo 2021](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2021.1898094) |
| 2-5 minutes between sets | Rest between sets with similar growth in trained men: In 13 strength-trained men, 2 and 5 minute rests gave similar muscle gains over three months. | Thin evidence | [Ahtiainen 2005](https://doi.org/10.1519/15604.1) |
| 5.6 weeks, average | Weeks between deloads reported by athletes: Reported by 246 strength and physique athletes. This is what they do, not what trials show is best. | Thin evidence | [Rogerson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00691-y) |
| 6.4 days, average | Typical deload length reported by athletes: Average length of a deload in the same survey of 246 strength and physique athletes. | Thin evidence | [Rogerson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00691-y) |
| -7.6 % performance change | Average performance change after short sleep: Pooled across 69 publications where sleep was 6 hours or less in 24 hours. | Some support | [Craven 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y) |
| 9.6 % over 8 weeks | Thigh muscle area gain in 8 weeks, sedentary men: Includes swelling in the first weeks. Typical for new lifters, not for trained ones. | Thin evidence | [DeFreitas 2011](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-011-1905-4) |

## Rep ranges and what each is good for

Approximate loads for each rep range, with what research suggests about the result. Percentages are rough and vary by person and lift.

| Reps per set | Rough load (% of 1RM) | What it is good for | Watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-5 | Over 85% | Maximal strength; practising heavy lifts | Long rests; technique slips when tired |
| 6-8 | About 75-85% | Strength and size; high-load range in Lopez 2021 | Joint load on heavy compounds |
| 8-12 | About 65-75% | Size; middle ground for most lifts | Stopping far from failure |
| 12-20 | About 55-65% | Size on single-joint and machine lifts | Pump and burn limiting sets before muscle is tired |
| 20-30 | About 30-50% | Size when taken to failure (49 trained men, 12 weeks) | Very hard sets; lower strength gains |

Some support · Sources: [Currier 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106807), [Lopez 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002585), [Refalo 2021](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2021.1898094), [Morton 2016](https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00154.2016)

## Training splits compared

Splits differ in how often each muscle is trained and how the week is arranged. With weekly volume equal, results were similar.

| Split | Days a week | Times each muscle is hit | Fits best | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full body | 2-4 | 2-4 | Beginners; busy people | Long sessions; fatigue from big lifts |
| Upper/lower | 4 | 2 | Most lifters at 4 days | Large sessions in the middle of the week |
| Push/pull/legs | 3 or 6 | 1 or 2 | People who enjoy daily training | 6 days a week is hard to sustain |
| Body-part split | 5-6 | 1 | Experienced lifters wanting high volume per muscle | Each muscle only once a week |
| Hybrid (upper/lower plus extras) | 4-5 | About 2 | People wanting variety | Needs more planning |

Some support · Sources: [Ramos-Campo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000004774), [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w), [Hamarsland 2022](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2021.789403)

## Rest between sets and sets per week: a guide

A reading of the research on rest and weekly sets. Treat each line as a starting point, then adjust to how you recover.

| Question | Starting point | What the evidence says |
|---|---|---|
| Heavy compound lift | 3-5 minutes | Held reps across sets on bench press (Senna 2016) |
| Single-joint, lighter lift | About 2 minutes | 2 minutes held reps on a chest fly (Senna 2016) |
| Short on time | Superset opposing muscles | Similar volume and gains, shorter sessions (Zhang 2025) |
| Weekly sets, general | At least 10 per muscle | Umbrella review: at least 10 sets is optimal |
| Weekly sets, trained men | 12-20 per muscle | Baz-Valle 2022; newer data show no clear ceiling |
| Rest vs growth | 2 or 5 minutes | Similar growth in trained men (Ahtiainen 2005) |

Some support · Sources: [Senna 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001142), [de Salles 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/11315230-000000000-00000), [Baz-Valle 2022](https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2022-0017), [Bernárdez-Vázquez 2022](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2022.949021), [Zhang 2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02176-8)

## Terms

- **Deload**: A period of reduced training stress meant to lower fatigue and prepare you for later training, as defined by a coach consensus.
- **Effect size and confidence interval**: Effect size is how big a difference is, in standard deviations. The interval shows a plausible range. If it spans zero, there is no clear difference.
- **Hard set**: A working set taken close to failure, usually within a few reps. Warm-up sets and easy sets do not count towards weekly volume.
- **Lengthened-position training**: Loading a muscle while it is stretched, as at the bottom of a curl or squat. Several trials found it grew more than loading it short.
- **Momentary muscular failure**: The point where you cannot finish another rep despite maximal effort. Volitional failure means you stop by choice.
- **One-rep max (1RM)**: The heaviest load you can lift for one full rep. Training loads are often given as a percent of it, such as 70% of 1RM.
- **Periodisation**: Planned changes in volume, load or exercises over weeks and months, such as linear steps or weekly undulation.
- **Progressive overload**: Gradually asking more of the muscle over time, by adding reps, load or sets, so it keeps having a reason to adapt.
- **Rate of perceived exertion (RPE)**: A 1-10 effort scale. On the RIR-based version, RPE 10 means 0 RIR, RPE 9 means 1 RIR, and so on.
- **Repetitions in reserve (RIR)**: The number of reps you could still have done when the set ended. 0 RIR means failure. 2 RIR means two more reps were possible.
- **Volume**: The amount of work. In this page, usually the number of hard sets per muscle per week. Volume load is sets times reps times weight.

---

Source page: https://kitesink.com/fitness#hypertrophy  
Maintained by Truman Kitos-Lindsey, KiteSink (https://kitesink.com).  
General information, not medical advice. Last updated 2026-11-15.

# Powerlifting: KiteSink fitness field guide

A bigger squat, bench press and deadlift. Each entry gives the point, the reasoning, what to do, how well supported it is, and its sources.

## Guidance

### Heavy loads build strength better than light loads

**For strength, heavy and moderate loads beat light loads, so most working sets should sit in the heavy to moderate range.**

A network meta-analysis of 28 studies in 747 healthy adults, all taken to failure, found muscle growth was similar across loads. Strength gains were larger with high loads (8 repetitions or fewer to failure) and moderate loads (9 to 15) than with low loads (over 15). High versus moderate was not clearly different. Light work still has a place for skill and recovery.

- Keep most working sets on the competition lifts in the 1-8 repetition range.
- Use light sets for warm-ups, skill work and easy days.

Percentages and zones · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Lopez 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002585)

### Practise the lifts in competition style and hold four principles

**Strength in the squat, bench press and deadlift is partly skill, so the lifts themselves, done to competition standard, make up most of the training.**

This is coaching convention, not a trial result. Train squat depth, the bench pause and the deadlift lockout the way they are judged. Four principles apply to all three lifts: a stable base, full-body tightness before the bar moves, a bar path close to a straight line over mid-foot, and the same set-up every rep. Assistance exercises support the lifts and do not replace them.

- Film your heaviest set of each lift every week, from the side.
- Use the same set-up routine on warm-ups and on heavy sets.

Technique and leverages · Beginner · Coaching practice

### RPE with reps in reserve lets you pick the load by feel

**A set rated RPE 9 left one repetition in reserve and RPE 10 left none; the scale worked on all three lifts in powerlifters.**

The scale pairs effort with repetitions in reserve (RIR): RPE 10 is 0 RIR and RPE 9 is 1 RIR. In 29 lifters, experienced squatters rated a 1RM higher than novices, and bar speed fell as RPE rose. In 15 powerlifters, RPE at 1RM was 9.6 to 9.7 on all three lifts, and RPE tracked percent of 1RM closely (r = 0.88 to 0.91).

- Rate each top set right after it ends, before looking at the bar speed or the numbers.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Zourdos 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001049), [Helms 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001517)

### Loading by RPE or bar speed works about as well as percentages

**Trials and a meta-analysis found no clear strength difference between autoregulated loading and fixed-percentage loading.**

A meta-analysis found no significant 1RM difference between autoregulated and standard percentage loading in resistance-trained people (mean difference 2.07 kg, 95% CI -0.32 to 4.46). In an 8-week trial of 21 trained men, RPE-based and percent-based loading both raised squat and bench press 1RM, and the gap between them was not significant. Both are valid ways to set load.

- Use RPE when daily readiness swings; use percentages when you want a fixed plan to compare weeks.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Hickmott 2022](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-021-00404-9), [Helms 2018](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.00247), [Larsen 2021](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.10663)

### Velocity loss limits did not change strength gains in a large review

**Ending a set when bar speed has dropped by a set percentage is a valid way to cap fatigue; the threshold changed strength little.**

A meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found the velocity loss chosen within sets did not change strength gains, while higher velocity loss went with more muscle growth. A second meta-analysis found thresholds of 25% or less gave slightly more 1RM strength (2.32 kg, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.31). Bar speed at 1RM differs by lift (0.23, 0.10 and 0.14 m/s for squat, bench and deadlift in 15 powerlifters), so each lift needs its own profile.

- Record bar speed on your own lifts for several weeks before using a velocity cut-off.

RPE and velocity · Advanced · Some support · Sources: [Jukic 2023](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01754-4), [Hickmott 2022](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-021-00404-9), [Helms 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001517)

### Strength does not need sets taken to failure

**Stopping sets short of failure gave similar strength gains to failure training, so heavy work can end with repetitions in reserve.**

A meta-analysis of 8 studies found non-failure training gave a 0.6 to 1.3% larger strength increase than failure training, a gap the authors judged unlikely to be meaningful. A later meta-regression found a negligible link between reps in reserve and strength gain, although muscle growth did show a negative slope with reps in reserve, meaning more growth nearer failure.

- Stop heavy sets with 1-3 repetitions in reserve; a missed rep costs recovery and, on the platform, a lift.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Davies 2016](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0451-3), [Robinson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02069-2)

### More weekly sets build more strength, with sharply diminishing returns

**Strength rises with weekly sets and with training frequency, but the gains flatten faster than muscle growth does.**

A meta-regression of 67 studies (2,058 participants) found strength gains rose with weekly set volume and with frequency, with diminishing returns that were more pronounced for strength than for muscle size. An earlier meta-analysis found high weekly sets beat low weekly sets (effect size 0.18), and a frequency meta-analysis found no significant effect once volume was equated.

- Add sets only when progress stalls, and add them to the lift that is lagging.

Frequency and volume · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w), [Ralston 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0762-7), [Ralston 2018](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-018-0149-9)

### A small dose of heavy work can still raise a powerlifter's 1RM

**About 3 to 6 heavy working sets per lift each week was enough to expect strength gains in powerlifters over 6 to 12 weeks.**

A multi-part study (interviews, surveys and two interventions with 25 intermediate to advanced powerlifters) proposed a minimum effective dose: about 3 to 6 working sets of 1 to 5 repetitions per lift each week, spread over 1 to 3 sessions, at loads above 80% of 1RM and RPE 7.5 to 9.5, for 6 to 12 weeks. It describes a floor for busy periods, not an ideal.

- Use this dose in busy or injured weeks, not as a long-term plan.

Frequency and volume · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Androulakis-Korakakis 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.713655)

### Training days per week usually rise with level

**Beginners do well on 2 to 3 sessions a week; advanced lifters often spread the lifts across 4 to 6.**

This is coaching convention. Beginners can practise each lift two or three times a week with little fatigue. Intermediates commonly train 3 to 4 days, with each lift twice a week. In a survey of 117 Norwegian powerlifters that included world, European and national champions, the most common answer (58.1%) was 5 to 6 sessions a week, with the most common load at 71-80% of 1RM.

- Add a session only when recovery between sessions is good and the lifts are improving.

Frequency and volume · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [Shaw 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003584)

### Planned variation beats a fixed routine for 1RM strength

**Periodised programs raised 1RM more than non-periodised ones, including when total volume was matched.**

A meta-analysis of 18 studies (81 effects) found periodised training gave larger 1RM gains than non-periodised training (effect size 0.43). A later meta-analysis of 35 volume-equated studies agreed for strength (effect size 0.31) but found no difference for muscle size. These trials were short, so the long-term picture in elite lifters is less clear.

- Change volume and intensity on a plan, not at random.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Williams 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0734-y), [Moesgaard 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01636-1)

### Linear, block and undulating plans differ little in trials

**No clear winner between linear and undulating models; too few trials exist to compare block models.**

Linear plans raise load week by week, block plans stack phases (volume, then intensity, then peaking), and daily undulating plans vary reps and load between sessions. A meta-analysis of 17 studies (510 participants) found no difference between linear and undulating for strength. A later one found a small edge for undulating in trained people (effect size 0.61, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.22) and could not compare other models.

- Pick the model you will follow for a full cycle and judge it on your own logbook.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Harries 2015](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000000712), [Moesgaard 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01636-1)

### Lifters taper for 5 to 10 days by cutting volume and keeping heavy singles

**Surveys report a short step taper: volume down about 40-50%, intensity kept high, last heavy squat and deadlift 7-10 days out.**

These are self-reports, not trials proving a taper works. In 364 North American raw powerlifters, a step taper over 7 to 10 days with 41-50% less volume was typical, with full rest about 2.8 days before the meet. A small trial of 19 athletes found 3 or 5 days of full rest kept lower-body strength; upper-body strength held at 3 days but not 5. A review found limited evidence that a short, heavy, low-volume session in the 48 hours before competition can help performance.

- Cut volume sharply but keep the competition lifts and a few heavy singles.
- Rest fully for the last 2 to 3 days before the meet.

Periodisation and peaking · Advanced · Thin evidence · Sources: [Travis 2021a](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004177), [Winwood 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-026-02500-w), [Travis 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004183), [Harrison 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-019-01136-3)

### Most strength athletes deload for about a week every 5 to 6 weeks

**Deloading is common but little tested: athletes cut sets and load, keep frequency and exercises, and add reps in reserve.**

An expert Delphi (34 coaches began, 21 finished the third round) defined a deload as a period of reduced training stress to mitigate fatigue and promote recovery. A survey of 246 strength and physique athletes found all deloaded, typically for 6.4 days every 5.6 weeks, keeping frequency and exercises. No trial has yet shown the best length or timing.

- Plan a lighter week roughly every 5 to 6 weeks, and move it earlier when joints ache and performance stalls.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Bell 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00633-0), [Rogerson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00691-y)

### Low-bar squats lean forward and load the hips; high-bar squats stay upright

**Bar position changes the squat: low-bar uses more hip and back, high-bar more knee and quadriceps.**

A review of back squat biomechanics found high-bar squats showed more knee bend, less hip bend, a more upright torso and greater depth. Low-bar squats showed more hip bend and forward lean, with more erector spinae, adductor and gluteal activity. A systematic review of classic powerlifting research suggested low-bar squats generally let lifters move more weight.

- Try each position for several weeks and keep the one you can repeat at competition depth.

Technique and leverages · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Glassbrook 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000002007), [Ferland 2019](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003099)

### Build the bench from the setup: tight back, planted feet, paused bar

**A stable arch and tight upper back shorten the bar path and make the pause on the chest repeatable.**

This is coaching convention. Keep head, shoulders and buttocks on the bench and feet flat on the floor. Pull the shoulder blades together and down, grip with the thumbs around the bar, and lower under control to the lower chest. Pause until the press command, then press back over the shoulders. Wider grips shorten the range, but federations cap grip width, so check the rulebook.

- Pause every training rep until the bar is still, and sometimes hold longer: the referee decides when to call 'Press'.

Technique and leverages · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [IPF 2026a](https://www.powerlifting.sport/rules/codes/info/technical-rules)

### Sumo and conventional deadlifts load the joints differently

**Sumo uses a wide stance and a more upright trunk; conventional moves the bar farther and does more mechanical work.**

In a video analysis of 12 sumo and 12 conventional lifters at a national championship, sumo lifters used a wider stance (70 cm against 32 cm; about 28 against 13 in), turned the feet out more and kept a more upright trunk. Bar distance, mechanical work and predicted energy cost were about 25 to 40% greater for conventional. The study did not test which style lifts more.

- Test both styles for a few weeks and keep the one that moves more weight with a steady back.

Technique and leverages · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Escamilla 2000](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-200007000-00013)

### Limb and torso lengths change which set-up suits you

**Proportions shift the best stance, depth and grip, so copy principles from top lifters and not their exact positions.**

This is coaching convention, not a tested rule. Long thighs relative to the torso tend to lean the squat forward and favour a wider stance. Long arms shorten the pull in the deadlift and lengthen the bench press path; short arms do the reverse. Use these as starting guesses and let filmed sets and bar speed decide.

- Film from the side and compare two set-ups on the same weight before changing for good.

Technique and leverages · Intermediate · Coaching practice

### Choose accessories for the point where the lift slows or fails

**Find where the bar slows, then train the muscles and positions that fail there with 1 to 3 exercises.**

A review describes the sticking point as the position in the range where difficulty rises disproportionately, and says working out its cause helps choose training. Powerlifters in a minimum-dose study typically used 1 to 3 accessory exercises per lift at RPE 7 to 9 and about 6 to 10 repetitions.

- Film a slow or missed rep, locate the sticking point, then pick exercises that train that range.

Accessories and bands · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Kompf 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-016-0615-9), [Androulakis-Korakakis 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.713655)

### Bands and chains help trained lifters when loads are 80% of 1RM or more

**In a meta-analysis, variable resistance beat constant resistance for trained lifters at 80% of 1RM and above.**

A meta-analysis of 14 studies found variable-resistance training (bands or chains) beat constant resistance for maximum strength (effect size 0.80). In trained people the benefit appeared at 80% of 1RM or more (0.76) and not below (0.00). In surveys, 39% of 28 elite British lifters used bands and 57% chains, and 76.9% of 117 Norwegian lifters used variable resistance.

- Add bands or chains to heavy work once the base technique is stable.

Accessories and bands · Advanced · Some support · Sources: [Lin 2022](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19148559), [Swinton 2009](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e31819424bd), [Shaw 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003584)

### Pick the class you can hold in training; move up when cutting costs lifts

**A lifter whose normal weight sits at a class limit can compete there with little cutting; large cuts are a reason to move up.**

This is coaching convention. Consider moving up when making weight takes more than a modest, gradual diet, when training quality drops in the weeks before weigh-in, or when you are growing into the next class anyway. An ACSM consensus statement on weight-category sports advises classifying athletes by preseason body composition and shortening the gap between weigh-in and competition.

- Weigh yourself in the morning for several weeks and compare the trend with the class limit.

Weight class and cutting · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [Burke 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/JSR.0000000000000831)

### Rapid weight cuts are common in powerlifting, and fluid loss costs strength

**Many lifters cut weight, mostly by fluid methods; fluid loss lowers strength and can harm health.**

Among 64 lifters at the 2018 IPF classic worlds, 83% cut weight (average 2.9% of body mass) and most reported negative effects on mood. In a survey of 321 lifters, 85.8% used rapid weight loss, and doctors and dietitians were rarely an influence. A meta-analysis of 28 manuscripts found hypohydration cut muscle strength by 5.5% on average. Extreme cuts can harm health; involve a sports dietitian or a doctor.

- Do not use fluid restriction, sauna or laxatives to make weight.
- Ask a sports dietitian or doctor before any planned weight loss.

Weight class and cutting · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Kwan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004199), [Nolan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003488), [Savoie 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0349-0)

### Short sleep lowers performance, with evening sessions hit harder

**A meta-analysis found sleep loss cut exercise performance by about 7.6% on average.**

Across 69 publications, sleep loss (6 hours or less in 24) lowered performance by a mean of 7.56% (95% CI -11.9 to -3.13), including strength tasks. Tests done in the morning were largely unaffected; those done in the evening were consistently worse. A systematic review of 17 studies found several nights of restricted sleep could cut force in compound lifts.

- Protect sleep in the week before a meet and keep a normal bedtime.

Recovery and injuries · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Craven 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y), [Knowles 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2018.01.012)

### Injury rates look low, but most lifters report pain in the back, shoulder or hip

**Counted as time lost, injuries are infrequent; counted as pain that affects training, most lifters have one.**

A systematic review of 9 studies found 1.0 to 4.4 injuries per 1,000 training hours in powerlifting, with the spine, shoulder and knee most affected. A survey of 104 Swedish subelite lifters counted pain or impaired function and found 70% currently injured and 87% injured in the past year, mostly lumbopelvic, shoulder and hip; only 16% of those currently injured stopped training completely.

- See a physio or doctor for pain that lasts more than a week, and adjust loads while it settles.

Recovery and injuries · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Aasa 2017](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096037), [Strömbäck 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/2325967118771016)

## Common mistakes

### Testing a true max every few weeks

**Frequent max attempts add fatigue and risk without adding much information.**

This is coaching convention. A true max is the heaviest single you can complete with legal technique. It is a hard, slow-to-recover effort, and a bad day gives a misleading number. Work from a training max set from recent RPE 8 to 9 sets, and keep true maxes for meets or planned tests every few months.

- Test at a meet or a planned test day, not on impulse.

Percentages and zones · Intermediate · Coaching practice

### Running percentages off an old or lucky max

**A percentage is only as good as the max behind it, so reset the number when strength changes.**

This is coaching convention. If the max is months old, the percentages are too light or too heavy, and a lucky one-off single makes the plan too hard to finish. Reps at a given percentage also vary between lifters, so use RPE alongside the plan and rebase when weights feel clearly off.

- Rebase percentages after every cycle using your best recent set, not one lucky rep.

Percentages and zones · Beginner · Coaching practice

### Treating RPE as exact when most lifters misjudge reps in reserve

**People tend to underpredict reps left in the tank, so RPE is a rough guide that improves with practice.**

A meta-analysis of 12 studies (414 participants) found people underpredicted repetitions to failure by 0.95 reps on average, with wide variation. Accuracy improved when the prediction was made nearer failure, with heavier loads and in later sets. A set called RPE 8 may have been closer to RPE 9.

- Calibrate by comparing your RPE with bar speed or filmed sets over several weeks.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Halperin 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01559-x)

### Cutting weight with fluid restriction in the last days

**Fluid restriction is a common but risky way to make weight, and it lowers strength and endurance.**

In the 2018 IPF classic worlds survey, fluid restriction after fluid loading was among the most common methods, used by about a third of lifters, alongside fasting and laxatives. A meta-analysis found hypohydration lowered muscle strength by 5.5% and muscle endurance by 8.3%. Where weigh-in is within about two hours of lifting, there is little time to recover.

- Stay near your class limit with normal eating, and see a sports dietitian before any cut.

Weight class and cutting · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Savoie 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0349-0), [Kwan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004199)

### Changing technique, equipment or exercises in the final weeks

**Late novelty brings soreness and risk with no time to adapt; keep the final weeks specific and familiar.**

This is coaching convention, and tapering interviews match it. Ten Croatian champions reported taper training that was highly specific, with assistance exercises removed and the same equipment as in competition. New Zealand elite lifters said poor tapers happened when they took a week or more off.

- Wear competition gear in the last heavy sessions and drop new exercises.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [Grgic 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001699), [Pritchard 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001292)

## Key numbers

| Number | What it is | Support | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~5 reps (most lifts) | Repetitions possible at 90% of 1RM: Typical maximum reps at 90% 1RM across exercises; the bench press averaged about 4. | Well supported | [Nuzzo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7) |
| ~14 reps (bench press) | Repetitions possible at 70% of 1RM on the bench: Typical maximum reps for the bench press at 70% 1RM; about 9 at 80% and about 4 at 90%. | Well supported | [Nuzzo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7) |
| 2.5 reps (SD) | Spread in reps between lifters at 80% of 1RM: The between-lifter standard deviation at 80% 1RM is 2.51 reps, so the same percentage gives different rep counts. | Well supported | [Nuzzo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7) |
| 40-50 % less volume | Volume cut during a taper: Surveyed North American powerlifters cut volume by 41-50%; a review of self-reported tapers gave about 40-45%. | Thin evidence | [Travis 2021a](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004177), [Winwood 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-026-02500-w) |
| 7-10 days before the meet | Last heavy squat and deadlift before a meet: Most surveyed North American raw lifters did their final heavy squat and deadlift 7 to 10 days out; bench came later. | Thin evidence | [Travis 2021a](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004177) |
| 3-6 sets per lift per week | Weekly working sets for a minimum effective dose: A floor proposed for powerlifters: 3 to 6 sets of 1 to 5 reps per lift, at loads above 80% 1RM, for 6 to 12 weeks. | Thin evidence | [Androulakis-Korakakis 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.713655) |
| 6.4 days (every 5.6 weeks) | Typical deload length: Average deload length reported by 246 competitive strength and physique athletes, taken about every 5.6 weeks. | Thin evidence | [Rogerson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00691-y) |
| 83 % of 64 lifters | Lifters who cut weight at the 2018 IPF classic worlds: Cutters lost an average of 2.9% of body mass; most reported negative mood effects. | Some support | [Kwan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004199) |
| 5.5 % lower muscle strength | Strength lost with hypohydration: Average fall in muscle strength with hypohydration in a meta-analysis of 28 manuscripts; endurance fell 8.3%. | Some support | [Savoie 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0349-0) |
| 35 years (SD 7) | Mean age of peak performance in world-class powerlifters: From world championship results 2003-2017; powerlifters peaked about 9 years later than weightlifters. | Some support | [Solberg 2019](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2019-0093) |

## Intensity zones as a percent of 1RM

Common coaching zones with typical reps per set and their purpose; reps at a given percentage vary by lifter.

| Zone | % of 1RM | Typical reps per set | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light | 50-65% | 8-12 or more | Warm-ups, skill work, easy days |
| Moderate | 65-75% | 5-8 | Volume work and technique practice |
| Working | 75-85% | 3-6 | Main strength work |
| Heavy | 85-92% | 1-3 | Heavy strength work, peaking blocks, openers |
| Near-max | 92-100% | 1 | Singles, tests, second and third attempts |

Coaching practice · Sources: [Nuzzo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7), [Travis 2021b](https://doi.org/10.1177/0031512520967608), [Howells 2022](https://doi.org/10.23736/S0022-4707.21.12140-1)

## RPE to reps in reserve chart

RPE 5 to 10 matched to repetitions in reserve (RIR); 9.5 is a half step many lifters add.

| RPE | Reps in reserve | What it feels like | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 0 | No repetition left; a true limit | Max attempts, 1RM tests |
| 9.5 | 0-1 | No rep left, but you could add a little load | Heavy top singles |
| 9 | 1 | One more repetition was possible | Heavy top sets |
| 8 | 2 | Two more possible; bar speed still decent | Main working sets |
| 7 | 3 | Three more possible; fast and controlled | Volume work, easier days |
| 5-6 | 4-6 | Light; plenty left | Warm-ups, technique work |

Some support · Sources: [Zourdos 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001049), [Helms 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000218)

## A 12-week cycle outline

A common layout from base volume to meet week; adjust loads by RPE and your own recovery.

| Weeks | Phase | Main work | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-4 | Accumulation | More sets and reps at 65-80% of 1RM | RPE 6-8 |
| 5-8 | Intensification | Fewer reps at 75-90%; competition-style lifts | RPE 7-9 |
| 9-10 | Peaking | Heavy doubles and singles at 85-95%; practise commands | RPE 8-9 |
| 11 | Taper | Volume down 40-50%; last heavy squat and deadlift | RPE 7-8 |
| 12 | Meet week | Short, light sessions early; rest the last 2-3 days | RPE 5-7 |

Coaching practice

## Terms

- **Accessory exercise**: An exercise outside the three competition lifts, chosen to build a muscle or fix a weak point.
- **Daily undulating periodisation (DUP)**: A plan that varies rep ranges and loads between sessions within the week, such as heavy, medium and light days.
- **Deload**: A planned lighter week or block, with less volume or load, to clear fatigue between harder blocks.
- **One-repetition maximum (1RM)**: The heaviest weight you can lift once with legal technique; the base for percentage programming.
- **Rating of perceived exertion (RPE)**: A 1 to 10 rating of how hard a set was; in strength training it is tied to how many repetitions were left.
- **Repetitions in reserve (RIR)**: How many more clean repetitions you could have done when the set ended; 2 RIR means two more were possible.
- **Sticking point**: The position in a lift where the bar slows most or where failures happen.
- **Taper (peaking)**: A planned drop in training stress, mostly volume, in the last days or weeks before a meet so fatigue clears and strength shows.
- **Velocity-based training (VBT)**: Setting load or stopping sets from measured bar speed, using a device that reports mean concentric velocity in metres per second.
- **Working max (training max)**: A weight you can repeat on a normal day, often set below a true max, and used as the base for training percentages.
