# Diet: KiteSink fitness field guide

Losing or gaining weight on purpose. Each entry gives the point, the reasoning, what to do, how well supported it is, and its sources.

## Guidance

### The 3,500 kcal per pound rule is a rough guide that varies with body fat

**About 3,500 kcal (7,700 per kg) per pound of loss is only an average, and leaner people need less per unit lost.**

The rule says a cumulative deficit of 3,500 kcal equals one pound (32.2 MJ per kg) of weight loss. A model found it approximately matches obese people with more than 30 kg of body fat, and it overestimates the deficit needed for people with less body fat. Weight also responds slowly: the half time was about one year in a separate model. Use it to size a plan, then correct against the scale.

- Use the rule to pick a starting deficit, then check the trend over three to four weeks.

Deficit and rate of loss · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Hall 2008](https://doi.org/10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720), [Hall 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X)

### Aim to lose about 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week

**A pace of 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week is the usual advice for keeping muscle while getting leaner.**

A contest-prep review recommends 0.5 to 1 percent a week, and a later review prefers 0.5 percent or less for attenuating fat-free mass loss. In 24 athletes, both groups lost about 5.5 percent of body weight, but the 0.7 percent weekly group gained 2.1 percent lean mass and lost 31 percent of fat mass, while the group set 1.4 percent (1.0 percent achieved) kept lean mass unchanged and lost 21 percent of fat mass. At 80 kg (176 lb), 0.5 to 1 percent is 0.4 to 0.8 kg (0.9 to 1.8 lb).

- Pick a weekly percentage, convert it to kg or lb, and check against your four-week trend.

Deficit and rate of loss · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Helms 2014b](https://doi.org/10.1186/1550-2783-11-20), [Garthe 2011](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97), [Roberts 2020](https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2019-0096)

### Deficits much beyond 500 kcal a day cost lean mass in lifters

**In a meta-regression, a deficit of about 500 kcal a day stopped lean-mass gains from training, while strength held up.**

A systematic review and meta-analysis of resistance training in an energy deficit found lean-mass gains were impaired against training without a deficit (effect size -0.57), but strength gains were comparable. The meta-regression put the point where gains were prevented at roughly 500 kcal a day. For people trying to preserve lean mass rather than add it, the authors advise avoiding deficits above that size. Short trials can differ: 40 young men on a 40 percent deficit with intense training gained 1.2 kg of lean mass on 2.4 g/kg of protein in 4 weeks.

- Keep deficits at or below about 500 kcal a day if gaining or keeping muscle is the priority.

Deficit and rate of loss · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Murphy 2022](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14075), [Longland 2016](https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.115.119339)

### Eat more protein when you diet: about 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of lean mass

**Lean lifters in a deficit kept more muscle with higher protein, around 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass.**

A review of six studies in lean, resistance-trained athletes in a deficit put protein needs at 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass, scaled up with the severity of the deficit and the leanness. The ISSN position gives 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of body weight. In a 4-week trial of 40 young men on a large deficit, 2.4 g/kg gained 1.2 kg of lean mass against 0.1 kg on 1.2 g/kg. A meta-analysis of 24 trials found higher protein held on to 0.43 kg more fat-free mass.

- Set protein by your lean mass, and move up as the diet gets harder and you get leaner.

Keeping muscle · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Helms 2014a](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054), [Jäger 2017](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8), [Longland 2016](https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.115.119339), [Wycherley 2012](https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.112.044321)

### Keep lifting while dieting, because training tells the body to keep muscle

**Resistance training reduced the lean mass lost in a diet, and strength was largely kept in deficit trials.**

An overview of 12 systematic reviews (149 studies) found resistance training limited lean mass loss during weight loss by about 0.8 kg. In six trials of older adults with obesity, training offset about 93 percent of the lean mass lost to calorie restriction. Strength gains in the deficit trials were comparable with and without a deficit.

- Keep the main lifts heavy, and drop sets before you drop load.

Keeping muscle · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Bellicha 2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/obr.13256), [Sardeli 2018](https://doi.org/10.3390/nu10040423), [Murphy 2022](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14075)

### Short sleep shifts diet loss toward muscle and away from fat

**In ten adults, five and a half hours of sleep cut the fat share of weight lost by 55 percent.**

Ten overweight adults ate a reduced-calorie diet for 14 days in two conditions, with 8.5 or 5.5 hours in bed. Short sleep cut the fraction of weight lost as fat by 55 percent (1.4 vs 0.6 kg) and increased loss of fat-free mass by 60 percent (1.5 vs 2.4 kg). Hunger rose too. It is a very small and short crossover study, so treat it as a strong hint and not a finding.

- Protect seven to nine hours in bed while dieting.

Keeping muscle · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Nedeltcheva 2010](https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-153-7-201010050-00006)

### Protein and unprocessed food help control hunger, at least in the short run

**Protein reduced hunger in meal studies, and a ward trial found unprocessed meals led to about 500 kcal less intake.**

A meta-analysis of 49 acute studies found protein lowered hunger and raised fullness, but long-term trials were inconclusive. In a ward study of 20 adults, ultra-processed meals led to 508 kcal a day more intake than unprocessed meals matched on presented calories, sugar, fibre and sodium, with weight up 0.9 kg against down 0.9 kg over two weeks. That is one small, short crossover trial.

- Build meals around protein and whole foods before cutting portion size.

Hunger and fullness · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Kohanmoo 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physbeh.2020.113123), [Hall 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008)

### Appetite rises as you lose weight, so hunger is part of the process

**In one 52-week trial, appetite rose enough to add about 100 kcal a day per kg of weight lost.**

In 153 people losing weight without being aware of the deficit, a model found eating drifted above baseline by about 100 kcal a day for each kilogram lost, more than three times the matching fall in energy expenditure. This is one analysis of one drug trial. It points to appetite, not metabolism, as the main pressure against keeping weight off.

- Plan for hunger to rise late in a diet, and use protein, fibre and a fixed end date.

Hunger and fullness · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Polidori 2016](https://doi.org/10.1002/oby.21653)

### Water-rich fruit and vegetables lower hunger for the same calories

**In one year-long trial, women who ate more water-rich foods lost more weight and reported less hunger.**

In 97 women with obesity told to cut fat, one group was also told to eat more water-rich foods, mainly fruit and vegetables, with no calorie goal. Among completers after a year, that group lost 7.9 kg against 6.4 kg, ate a greater weight of food at a lower energy density, and reported less hunger. It is one trial in women with obesity, not lifters.

- Fill half the plate with vegetables or fruit before adding the rest.

Hunger and fullness · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [Ello-Martin 2007](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/85.6.1465), [Hall 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008)

### Metabolic slowdown with dieting is real but smaller than most people fear

**Adaptation is real but small, tens to low hundreds of kcal a day in most studies, so check your log first.**

A systematic review of 33 studies (2,528 participants) found adaptive thermogenesis in 27, with lower or non-significant values in the better-designed studies. In 171 women, the drop after loss was 54 kcal a day, and in a subset of 46 it was no longer significant at one and two years. In 32 men on a 50 percent deficit for three weeks, true adaptation was 72 kcal a day. After 6 years, 14 Biggest Loser contestants were 499 kcal a day below prediction, an extreme case.

- Check the log and weekends before blaming metabolism.

Scale, plateaus and metabolism · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Nunes 2022a](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007114521001094), [Martins 2020](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/nqaa086), [Müller 2015](https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.115.109173), [Fothergill 2016](https://doi.org/10.1002/oby.21538)

### Day-to-day weight changes are mostly water, so read the trend

**Two-week changes of 1 to 3 kg were largely fat-free mass and water, not fat, in free-living adults.**

In 46 adults, a unit of two-week weight change was 84 percent fat-free mass, and the energy density of 1 to 3 kg changes was about 2,380 kcal per kg, well below that of fat. Glycogen is stored with three to four parts water. Weight runs higher on Sunday and Monday in 80 adults, and fluid retention peaks at the start of menstrual flow in 62 women. None of these is fat gain.

- Weigh at the same time under the same conditions, and judge the weekly average.
- If you menstruate, compare the same week of one cycle with the same week of the next.

Scale, plateaus and metabolism · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Bhutani 2017](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.13336), [Kreitzman 1992](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/56.1.292S), [Orsama 2014](https://doi.org/10.1159/000356147), [White 2011](https://doi.org/10.1155/2011/138451)

### A two-week stall is not proof your diet stopped working

**Check logging and weekend intake before cutting calories, since stalls are usually noise or under-logging.**

Ten people who reported not losing weight on under 1,200 kcal actually under-reported intake by 47 percent and over-reported activity by 51 percent. In a one-year trial of 48 adults, calorie-restricted participants stopped losing weight on weekends. Add water noise from the table above and a two-week stall tells you little. A real stall holds over three to four weeks of honest logging.

- Wait three to four weeks, then cut by about 100 to 200 kcal or add steps.

Scale, plateaus and metabolism · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Lichtman 1992](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199212313272701), [Racette 2008](https://doi.org/10.1038/oby.2008.320), [Bhutani 2017](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.13336)

### Weighing yourself regularly goes with more loss inside a programme

**Programmes that included self-weighing beat minimal care by 3.4 kg, and daily weighing did no better than weekly.**

A meta-analysis found 15 trials of multi-component programmes that included self-weighing lost 3.4 kg more than minimal or no intervention, with no significant difference between daily and weekly weighing. Only one study tested self-weighing alone, and it found no evidence of an effect. The scale works as a feedback tool inside a plan, not as a plan.

- Weigh on a fixed schedule, then act on the weekly average.

Scale, plateaus and metabolism · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Madigan 2015](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-015-0267-4)

### Diet breaks and refeeds give mixed fat-loss results and may ease hunger

**Planned weeks at maintenance did not improve fat loss in lifters, and they lowered hunger.**

In 61 resistance-trained adults over 12 weeks, alternating three weeks of restriction with one week at maintenance gave the same fat and lean mass as continuous dieting, with lower hunger. A meta-analysis of 12 trials (881 participants) found the same body composition and a smaller drop in resting rate. A small 7-week trial found a weekly two-day carb refeed kept more lean mass (-0.4 vs -1.3 kg). Results in men with obesity favoured breaks.

- Try a one- to two-week break at maintenance if hunger or training quality is slipping.

Diet type and meal pattern · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [PEOS 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000002636), [Poon 2025](https://doi.org/10.1093/nutrit/nuad168), [Campbell 2020](https://doi.org/10.3390/jfmk5010019), [Byrne 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/ijo.2017.206)

### The best diet is the one you can keep to, since types differ little

**Low-carb and low-fat diets lost about the same weight, so pick the one you can keep.**

A network meta-analysis of 48 randomized trials (7,286 people) found weight loss with any low-carbohydrate or low-fat diet, with small differences among named diets. A larger analysis of 121 trials (21,942 patients) found about 4.6 kg at 6 months with low carb and 4.4 kg with low fat. In a 12-month trial of 609 adults, the difference was 0.7 kg, not significant. Behavioural support added about 3.2 kg at six months in one analysis.

- Choose the pattern that fits your food preferences and schedule.

Diet type and meal pattern · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Johnston 2014](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2014.10397), [Ge 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.m696), [Gardner 2018](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.0245)

### Intermittent fasting works by eating less, with no clear extra effect

**Time-restricted eating did not beat plain calorie control in long trials, though one pooled analysis disagrees.**

In 139 adults over 12 months, eating 8 am to 4 pm with calorie restriction lost 8.0 kg against 6.3 kg for calorie restriction alone, not a significant difference. A 12-week trial of 116 people found no advantage, and a 41-person feeding trial matched calories and found no effect on weight. A pooled analysis of 30 studies did report 1.46 kg more loss in matched comparisons. With lifting, an analysis of eight studies (221 participants) kept fat-free mass.

- Use a fasting window only if it makes eating less easier for you.

Diet type and meal pattern · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Liu 2022](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114833), [Lowe 2020](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153), [Maruthur 2024](https://doi.org/10.7326/M23-3132), [Fernandes-Alves 2026](https://doi.org/10.1093/nutrit/nuaf053), [Ashtary-Larky 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physbeh.2021.113453), [Keenan 2020](https://doi.org/10.3390/nu12082349)

### Meal frequency and late eating matter little for fat loss at equal calories

**Differences between meal patterns are small at equal calories; fewer meals showed about 1 kg more loss in one analysis.**

A network meta-analysis of 22 trials (647 people) found two meals a day slightly lowered weight against three meals or six, by about 1 kg, under equal calories. In 16 obese adults on the same deficit, three meals and three snacks did no better than three meals. A meta-analysis of 9 trials found earlier eating gave 1.2 kg more loss, and a controlled crossover trial found late eating raised hunger. Pick the pattern you can follow.

- Choose a meal pattern around your day, and keep protein in each meal.

Diet type and meal pattern · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Schwingshackl 2020](https://doi.org/10.1093/advances/nmaa056), [Cameron 2010](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007114509992984), [Young 2023](https://doi.org/10.1111/obr.13537), [Vujović 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2022.09.007)

### Weight lost tracked sticking to the diet, not which diet it was

**In one year-long trial, weight lost followed how closely people kept to their diet, with no link to the diet they chose.**

In 160 overweight or obese adults with heart-risk factors, assigned to Atkins, Zone, Weight Watchers or Ornish, mean one-year loss was 2.1 to 3.3 kg and only 50 to 65 percent finished. Loss correlated with self-reported adherence (r = 0.60) but not with diet type (r = 0.07). Adherence was self-reported and chosen by the participants, so this shows who did well, not that pushing adherence causes loss.

- Pick the eating pattern you can see yourself keeping for a year.

Diet type and meal pattern · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Dansinger 2005](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.293.1.43), [Johnston 2014](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2014.10397)

### Exercise adds to fat loss, and daily movement drops on diets if you let it

**Exercise adds 1.5 to 3.5 kg of loss in reviews, and people on diets may move less outside the gym.**

An overview of 12 meta-analyses found exercise led to 1.5 to 3.5 kg of weight loss and similar results from aerobic and interval training when energy expenditure matched. The ACSM suggests 150 minutes a week as a floor and 200 to 300 for long-term loss. A systematic review of 36 articles found lower non-exercise activity in 63 percent of diet-only arms. In 16 overfed adults, NEAT explained the large differences in fat gain.

- Set a daily step or activity floor and keep it during the diet.

Cardio and daily movement · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Bellicha 2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/obr.13256), [DONNELLY 2009](https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181949333), [Silva 2018](https://doi.org/10.1017/S000711451800096X), [Levine 1999](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.283.5399.212)

### Getting very lean costs hormones, mood and training quality, so go carefully

**Prolonged energy availability under about 25 kcal per kg of lean mass in men led to muscle loss and hormonal and mood problems; in women, hormones were disrupted below 30.**

Reviews of lean athletes link a long period at low energy availability to muscle loss, hormone disruption and psychological problems. A case study of one natural bodybuilder saw body fat fall from 14.8 to 4.5 percent and testosterone from 9.22 to 2.27 ng/mL, recovering after the contest. In 27 women dieting for a fitness show, sex hormones fell and menstrual irregularities rose, and most recovered within three to four months. Involve a coach and clinician.

- Treat contest-level leanness as a short, supervised project, not a lifestyle.
- See a clinician if periods stop or mood drops.

Very lean, regain and maintenance · Advanced · Some support · Sources: [Fagerberg 2018](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.2016-0332), [Rossow 2013](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.8.5.582), [Hulmi 2017](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2016.00689), [Loucks 2003](https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2002-020369), [Mountjoy 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994), [Helms 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports7070172)

### Weight regain is common, and maintenance is possible with sustained habits

**Most people regain some weight, and a minority keep most of it off by staying active and weighing themselves.**

In 171 women, participants regained 52 percent of the weight lost at one year and 89 percent at two. A meta-analysis of 29 US studies found that after five years the average person kept off more than 3 kg. Among 2,886 National Weight Control Registry members, mean loss was 31.3 kg at entry and 23.1 kg at ten years. They report about an hour of activity a day, regular weighing and consistent eating on weekends. The registry is self-selected.

- After the diet, raise calories in steps and keep weighing weekly.
- Keep activity and protein high.

Very lean, regain and maintenance · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Martins 2020](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/nqaa086), [Anderson 2001](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/74.5.579), [Thomas 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2013.08.019), [Wing 2005](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/82.1.222S), [Hall 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcna.2017.08.012), [Rosenbaum 2010](https://doi.org/10.1038/ijo.2010.184)

### A small surplus adds muscle, and a large surplus mostly adds fat

**A surplus of about 10 to 20 percent over maintenance is a common starting range for lifters, and nobody has proven the best size.**

A narrative review for physique athletes suggests 10 to 20 percent above maintenance, with advanced lifters more conservative. In 17 lifters over 8 weeks, a 15 percent surplus mainly increased fat gain rather than strength or muscle thickness. Another review finds the ideal surplus is unknown. If maintenance is 2,500 kcal, 10 to 20 percent is 250 to 500 kcal. Evidence is thin and short.

- Start near the low end of the surplus and adjust to the scale.

Gaining phases · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Iraki 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports7070154), [Helms 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00651-y), [Slater 2019](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2019.00131)

### Recomposition works best for beginners, returners and people carrying more fat

**Gaining muscle while losing fat is realistic with high protein and hard training, and likely harder for lean, advanced lifters.**

In 40 young men on a roughly 40 percent deficit with heavy training and 2.4 g/kg of protein, lean mass rose 1.2 kg while fat mass fell 4.8 kg over four weeks. A review of six studies found that the groups that held on to or gained lean mass were among those with the highest body fat, the smallest deficit or a new training stimulus. Advanced lifters with low body fat have less room.

- Use a small deficit or maintenance with high protein and progressive training.

Gaining phases · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Longland 2016](https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.115.119339), [Helms 2014a](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054), [Murphy 2022](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14075)

## Common mistakes

### Dieting faster than 1 percent of body weight a week

**Faster loss gave up the lean-mass gain seen with slower loss in athletes, and the speed is hard to keep up.**

In 24 athletes lifting four times a week, a group set to lose 1.4 percent a week (1.0 percent achieved) kept lean mass unchanged and cut fat mass 21 percent, while a 0.7 percent loss gained 2.1 percent lean mass and cut fat mass 31 percent. Reviews recommend 0.5 to 1 percent a week.

- Slow the deficit to 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week.

Deficit and rate of loss · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Garthe 2011](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97), [Helms 2014b](https://doi.org/10.1186/1550-2783-11-20)

### Cutting protein and stopping lifting while dieting

**The two habits that protect muscle in a deficit are protein and heavy training, and dropping both costs lean mass.**

Higher protein held on to lean mass in trials of lean lifters, and training reduced lean loss by about 0.8 kg across an overview of reviews.

- Keep protein high and lifts heavy until the diet ends.

Keeping muscle · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Helms 2014a](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054), [Bellicha 2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/obr.13256)

### Cutting calories after a short stall

**Short stalls are mostly water and weekend noise, and cutting on them stacks deficit on top of a working plan.**

A two-week plateau can come from water, a missed weekend or logging drift, as 48 adults who stopped losing on weekends showed. Cutting calories on a stall moves you toward the 500 kcal limit sooner. Wait three to four weeks, check the log, and only then change calories or steps.

- Check the four-week trend and the log before changing calories.

Scale, plateaus and metabolism · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Racette 2008](https://doi.org/10.1038/oby.2008.320), [Bhutani 2017](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.13336), [Murphy 2022](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14075)

### Dieting with no end date and no plan for after

**Regain follows the diet for most people, and a plan for the exit matters as much as the deficit.**

In 171 women, 52 percent of lost weight was regained after one year and 89 percent after two. Registry members who kept it off kept activity, regular weighing and steady eating. Set an end date for the diet.

- Plan the exit: a target date, a maintenance range and a weekly weigh-in.
- Step calories up toward maintenance over several weeks.

Very lean, regain and maintenance · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Martins 2020](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/nqaa086), [Wing 2005](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/82.1.222S)

### Treating a gaining phase as a licence to eat anything

**A large surplus mainly added fat in a trial, and extra fat has to be dieted off later.**

In 17 lifters, a 15 percent surplus mostly increased fat gain rather than strength or muscle thickness. A review suggests 10 to 20 percent for physique athletes, less for advanced lifters. The extra fat then has to be dieted off.

- Use a measured surplus and watch the rate of weight gain.

Gaining phases · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Helms 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00651-y), [Iraki 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports7070154)

## Key numbers

| Number | What it is | Support | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5-1 % body weight per week | Rate of loss: Usual pace for keeping muscle; at 80 kg (176 lb) that is 0.4 to 0.8 kg a week. | Some support | [Helms 2014b](https://doi.org/10.1186/1550-2783-11-20), [Garthe 2011](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97) |
| 500 kcal per day | Deficit that stopped lean-mass gains: In a meta-regression, deficits around this size prevented gains in lean mass in people doing resistance training. | Well supported | [Murphy 2022](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14075) |
| 3,500 kcal per lb | Energy per pound of weight lost: The classic rule of thumb, which equals about 7,700 kcal per kg and varies with body fat. | Some support | [Hall 2008](https://doi.org/10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720) |
| 2.3-3.1 g per kg lean mass | Protein in a deficit: ISSN and review ranges for lean lifters dieting; raise it as the deficit and leanness grow. | Well supported | [Helms 2014a](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.2013-0054), [Jäger 2017](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8) |
| 100 kcal per day per kg | Appetite rise per kg of weight lost: In one trial, eating drifted above baseline by about this much for each kilogram lost. | Thin evidence | [Polidori 2016](https://doi.org/10.1002/oby.21653) |
| 2,380 kcal per kg | Energy per kg for short-term changes: Two-week changes of 1 to 3 kg were mostly fat-free mass and water, so they carry less energy than fat. | Some support | [Bhutani 2017](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.13336) |
| 10-20 % above maintenance | Surplus for a gaining phase: Suggested range for novice and intermediate lifters in a physique-sport review; advanced lifters go lower. | Thin evidence | [Iraki 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports7070154) |
| 0.25-0.5 % body weight per week | Rate of gain, novice to intermediate: At 80 kg (176 lb) that is 0.2 to 0.4 kg (0.4 to 0.9 lb) a week. | Thin evidence | [Iraki 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports7070154) |

## Deficit size versus expected weekly loss

Approximate weekly loss for a daily deficit at 7,700 kcal per kg (3,500 per lb), for an 80 kg (176 lb) person. Leaner people tend to lose more weight than this.

| Daily deficit | Weekly total | Loss per week | Share of 80 kg (176 lb) | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 250 kcal | 1,750 kcal | 0.23 kg (0.5 lb) | 0.3% | Slow; below the usual range |
| 500 kcal | 3,500 kcal | 0.45 kg (1.0 lb) | 0.6% | In range; near the limit seen for lean-mass trials |
| 750 kcal | 5,250 kcal | 0.68 kg (1.5 lb) | 0.85% | In range; hold protein and training high |
| 1,000 kcal | 7,000 kcal | 0.91 kg (2.0 lb) | 1.1% | Above 1%; faster than the athlete trial achieved |

Some support · Sources: [Hall 2008](https://doi.org/10.1038/sj.ijo.0803720), [Helms 2014b](https://doi.org/10.1186/1550-2783-11-20), [Murphy 2022](https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14075), [Garthe 2011](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97)

## What moves scale weight day to day

Short-term causes of scale changes that are not fat gain or loss.

| Cause | What happens | Time scale |
|---|---|---|
| Glycogen and water | Each gram of glycogen is stored with three to four parts water | Days, with carbohydrate changes |
| Weekly rhythm | Weight is higher on Sunday and Monday, then falls | Weekly |
| Menstrual cycle | Fluid retention scores peak on the first day of flow | Monthly |
| Short-term free-living change | 1-3 kg over two weeks is about 84% fat-free mass and water | Two weeks |
| Fat change | Slow; reviews advise about 0.5-1% of body weight a week | Weeks to months |

Some support · Sources: [Kreitzman 1992](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/56.1.292S), [Orsama 2014](https://doi.org/10.1159/000356147), [White 2011](https://doi.org/10.1155/2011/138451), [Bhutani 2017](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.13336), [Helms 2014b](https://doi.org/10.1186/1550-2783-11-20)

## Rate of gain by training age

Suggested pace of weight gain in a gaining phase; the research is thin and the rates are conservative.

| Lifter | Weekly rate | At 80 kg (176 lb) | Surplus | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Novice or intermediate | 0.25-0.5% a week | 0.2-0.4 kg (0.4-0.9 lb) | About 10-20% | Review suggestion for bodybuilders |
| Advanced | Lower than novice rate | Lower than the row above | Smaller than 10-20% | No studied figure; be conservative |
| Large surplus (15%) | Faster gain | More body mass | 15% above maintenance | Mostly extra fat in an 8-week trial |

Thin evidence · Sources: [Iraki 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports7070154), [Helms 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00651-y), [Slater 2019](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2019.00131)

## Terms

- **Adaptive thermogenesis (metabolic adaptation)**: A fall in energy use beyond what the loss of body mass explains, seen during and after weight loss. Studies find it ranges from small to modest.
- **Diet break and refeed**: A diet break is a planned stretch, often one to two weeks, at maintenance calories. A refeed is shorter, usually one or two days of higher carbohydrate.
- **Energy deficit**: Eating less energy than you use. It is the one requirement for losing body fat. A daily deficit of 500 kcal is about 3,500 kcal a week.
- **NEAT (non-exercise activity)**: Non-exercise activity thermogenesis: energy spent on walking, standing, fidgeting and chores. It can fall during a diet without you noticing.
- **Recomposition**: Gaining muscle and losing fat over the same period. Body weight may hold steady or fall while the body changes shape.
- **Set point and settling point**: Two models of body weight: a defended set point, or a settling point where weight drifts with food and activity. A review finds both incomplete.
- **Time-restricted eating**: Eating all meals within a set daily window, such as eight hours, and fasting for the rest. It is one form of intermittent fasting.

---

Source page: https://kitesink.com/fitness#diet  
Maintained by Truman Kitos-Lindsey, KiteSink (https://kitesink.com).  
General information, not medical advice. Last updated 2026-11-15.

================================================================
FILE: https://kitesink.com/fitness/health.md
================================================================

# Health: KiteSink fitness field guide

Training for a long working life. Each entry gives the point, the reasoning, what to do, how well supported it is, and its sources.

## Guidance

### WHO asks adults for 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week

**Aim for 150 to 300 minutes of moderate or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous aerobic activity a week, plus strength work on 2 or more days.**

The 2020 WHO guidelines give these ranges for all adults, with an equivalent mix of moderate and vigorous activity allowed. They also advise muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week. The US 2018 and UK 2019 guidelines set the same weekly minimums. Moderate means you can talk but not sing. Vigorous means you can say only a few words before a breath.

- Add up walks, rides and sessions across the week to reach the range.
- Place two strength sessions on separate days.

Activity guidelines · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [Bull 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955), [Piercy 2018](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.14854), [UCMO 2019](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/physical-activity-guidelines-uk-chief-medical-officers-report)

### Mortality benefit levelled off at about two to five times the minimum

**In large cohorts, the lowest death rates sat near 2 to 5 times the guideline minimum, with no clear harm at higher amounts.**

Arem 2015 pooled 661,137 adults and found a 31% lower mortality risk at 1 to 2 times the minimum and 37% at 2 to 3 times, with the best result near 3 to 5 times and no excess risk at 10 or more times. Lee 2022 followed 116,221 US health professionals and found the near-maximum association at about 150 to 300 minutes a week of vigorous or 300 to 600 of moderate activity. Both studies are observational and rely on self-reported activity.

- Treat 300 minutes a week of moderate activity as a ceiling for health benefit, not a requirement.

Activity guidelines · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Arem 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2015.0533), [Lee 2022](https://doi.org/10.1161/circulationaha.121.058162)

### Death risk in cohorts fell with daily steps and flattened around 5,000 to 8,000

**Cohort data show the steepest gains in the first thousands of steps, with 7,000 steps linked to about half the risk of 2,000.**

Paluch 2022 pooled 15 cohorts (47,471 adults): risk fell until about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day at age 60 and over and 8,000 to 10,000 under 60. Ding 2025 pooled 31 studies and found 7,000 steps a day linked to 47% lower all-cause mortality than 2,000 (HR 0.53). Evidence certainty was rated moderate. These are associations from device-measured cohorts.

- Use 7,000 steps as a realistic target and add more if it is easy.

Activity guidelines · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Paluch 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/s2468-2667(21)00302-9), [Ding 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/s2468-2667(25)00164-1)

### About an hour of daily moderate activity matched the extra risk from long sitting

**People who sat over 8 hours but did about 60 to 75 minutes of moderate activity a day showed no raised mortality risk.**

This pooled analysis covered 16 studies, and the sitting analysis used 13 of them with 1,005,791 people. Those sitting more than 8 hours a day with the highest activity level had a hazard ratio of 1.04 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.10) against the most active, least sedentary group. High TV time stayed linked to higher risk, though less so in the most active. Self-reported sitting is imprecise.

- Break up long sitting spells and fit in a daily walk or ride.

Activity guidelines · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Ekelund 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(16)30370-1)

### The talk test finds moderate effort without a lab

**If you can talk but not sing, you are in the moderate range, and if you can only say a few words, you are at vigorous effort.**

The talk test links speech to the ventilatory and lactate thresholds. A 2014 review describes it as valid, reliable and practical for healthy adults and heart patients, and comfortable speech is likely when you are below the threshold. The US guidelines give the same rule of thumb. The review notes it may not suit high-intensity intervals.

- Hold a steady pace where full sentences are easy.
- Slow down if you need to catch your breath mid-sentence.

Aerobic base and zone 2 · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Reed 2014](https://doi.org/10.1097/hco.0000000000000097), [Piercy 2018](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.14854)

### Zone 2 means effort just below the first lactate or ventilatory threshold

**Experts define zone 2 as easy aerobic work just under the first threshold, where breathing rises but speech stays comfortable.**

A 14-person panel of sport scientists and coaches agreed that zone 2 is best placed immediately below the first lactate or ventilatory threshold. The thresholds differ from person to person and shift with training. The panel said the adaptations are likely not unique to zone 2 and can occur a little above or below. This is expert opinion, not trial evidence.

- Start with the talk test to find a steady, conversational pace.

Aerobic base and zone 2 · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Sitko 2025](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2024-0303), [MacIntosh 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2021.682233)

### Evidence does not show zone 2 is the best intensity for health

**A 2025 review found no proof that zone 2 is optimal and argued harder work matters for health, especially at low weekly volumes.**

The review traced the zone 2 claims largely to observational data from elite endurance athletes who train a lot. It concluded the evidence does not support zone 2 as the optimal intensity for building mitochondrial or fat-burning capacity. It also said that higher intensities are important for cardiometabolic health when time is short. It is a narrative review, so it reflects the authors' reading.

- If time is short, keep some harder work in the week alongside easy sessions.

Aerobic base and zone 2 · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Storoschuk 2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02261-y), [Sitko 2025](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2024-0303)

### Interval training raised VO2 max slightly more than steady training in short trials

**Pooled trials show interval training lifts VO2 max a little more than continuous training, by roughly 1 to 3 mL/kg/min.**

In healthy young to middle-aged adults, the gain was a possibly small 1.2 mL/kg/min more than endurance training (Milanovic 2015). In 273 patients with cardiometabolic disease across 10 studies, interval training beat moderate continuous training by 3.03 mL/kg/min, or 9.1% (Weston 2014). Both reviews pool short trials.

- Add one interval session a week if your clinician agrees you can train hard.

Aerobic base and zone 2 · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Milanović 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0365-0), [Weston 2013](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2013-092576)

### Higher aerobic fitness goes with lower mortality, with no upper limit seen

**Across large cohorts, each 1 MET higher fitness was linked to 11% to 17% lower all-cause mortality, and the top fitness group did best.**

An umbrella review of 26 reviews found high versus low fitness linked to a hazard ratio of 0.47 for all-cause mortality, with evidence certainty from very low to moderate. Kodama 2009 found low fitness carried a relative risk of 1.70 against high fitness. In 122,007 treadmill-tested patients and 750,302 veterans, the lowest risk was in the fittest group, with no rise in risk at the top. These are observational findings, and fitter people may differ in other ways.

- Test your fitness over time with a repeatable walk, run or ride.

VO2 max and fitness · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Lang 2024](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-107849), [Mandsager 2018](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.3605), [Kokkinos 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2022.05.031), [Kodama 2009](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2009.681)

### Weaker grip strength tracks with higher risk of death in large cohorts

**Each 5 kg (11 lb) lower grip strength went with about 16% to 20% higher all-cause mortality risk, a marker and not a proven cause.**

In 139,691 adults in the PURE study, the hazard ratio per 5 kg lower grip was 1.16 for all-cause death. In half a million UK Biobank participants it was 1.20 in women and 1.16 in men. A meta-analysis of 38 studies found higher grip linked to lower mortality (HR 0.69). The authors say trials are still needed to show that raising strength lowers risk.

- Track grip or another strength test over time and ask a clinician about low results.

Strength and muscle · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Leong 2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(14)62000-6), [Celis-Morales 2018](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.k1651), [García-Hermoso 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apmr.2018.01.008)

### About 30 to 60 minutes a week of strength training was linked to the lowest mortality

**Pooled cohorts link any strength training to 10% to 17% lower mortality, with the best result near 30 to 60 minutes a week.**

Momma 2022 pooled 16 studies and found a J-shaped link, with the lowest risk at about 30 to 60 minutes a week. Shailendra 2022 pooled 10 studies and found 15% lower all-cause mortality for any resistance training, with a maximum reduction of 27% at about 60 minutes a week and smaller benefit at higher volumes. These are observational and training was self-reported.

- Start with 2 short strength sessions a week.

Strength and muscle · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Momma 2022](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105061), [Shailendra 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2022.03.020)

### Resistance training builds strength, muscle and function in older adults

**Progressive resistance training reliably improves strength and daily function in people aged 60 and over, and harder training works better.**

A Cochrane review found a large effect on strength (73 trials, 3,059 people, SMD 0.84) and improved physical function. A meta-analysis of 47 studies found harder training gave bigger strength gains. Another of 49 studies found an average lean mass gain of 1.1 kg, with higher volume helping. The NSCA position statement backs resistance training for older adults. Serious adverse events were rare.

- Begin with a supervised program if you are new or have health conditions.
- Raise the load gradually over weeks.

Strength and muscle · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Liu Cj 2009](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd002759.pub2), [Peterson 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.arr.2010.03.004), [PETERSON 2011](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0b013e3181eb6265), [Fragala 2019](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000003230)

### Strength falls two to five times faster than muscle size in later life

**At about age 75, strength drops about 2.5% to 4% a year while muscle mass drops under 1% a year.**

A review of longitudinal studies found muscle mass loss of 0.64% to 0.70% a year in women and 0.80% to 0.98% in men at age 75, with strength loss of 3% to 4% a year in men and 2.5% to 3% in women. Loss of strength carried a more consistent risk for disability and death than loss of muscle. The European consensus for sarcopenia now puts low strength first.

- Train strength, not only walking, to protect the quality that falls fastest.

Strength and muscle · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Mitchell 2012](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2012.00260), [Cruz-Jentoft 2018](https://doi.org/10.1093/ageing/afy169)

### Raising activity in midlife was linked to similar mortality benefit to lifelong activity

**Adults who stepped up activity between ages 40 and 61 had a mortality risk similar to those who were always active.**

In a US cohort, those who kept high leisure activity through adulthood had a hazard ratio of 0.64 for all-cause death compared with the consistently inactive. Those who were less active until they raised it at ages 40 to 61 had 0.65. This is observational. Trials in older adults show strength and function improve with resistance training.

- Begin now with a modest plan and build over months.

Strength and muscle · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Saint-Maurice 2019](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2019.0355), [Liu Cj 2009](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd002759.pub2)

### Exercise that challenges balance cuts falls by about a quarter in older adults at home

**Falls fall about 23% with exercise in community-dwelling older adults, and balance-challenging programs of over 3 hours a week did best.**

A Cochrane review of 108 trials (23,407 people, average age 76) found exercise reduced the rate of falls by 23% (rate ratio 0.77), with high-certainty evidence. An earlier meta-analysis found programs that challenged balance and ran over 3 hours a week gave a 39% cut. No effect was seen in aged care homes or after stroke. Most participants were women.

- Choose programs that include standing balance work, not only walking.
- Ask a physiotherapist or clinician to pick safe options if you have fallen.

Bones and balance · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Sherrington 2019](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd012424.pub2), [Sherrington 2016](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096547)

### LIFTMOR: supervised heavy lifting and impact work raised spine bone density

**In 101 postmenopausal women with low bone mass, eight months of supervised heavy lifting and impact work improved spine bone density.**

LIFTMOR gave 49 women twice-weekly 30-minute supervised sessions of 5 sets of 5 repetitions at over 85% of one-rep max, with impact loading, while 52 did a home low-intensity program. Lumbar spine density changed by +2.9% versus -1.2% and femoral neck by +0.3% versus -1.9%. One minor adverse event occurred. Women were screened and supervised, so this does not suit unsupervised heavy training. The UK consensus advises resistance and impact exercise for bone and avoiding deep spinal flexion. After a vertebral fracture, impact should usually stay near brisk walking.

- Discuss any heavy or impact work with a clinician and use qualified supervision.

Bones and balance · Advanced · Thin evidence · Sources: [Watson 2017](https://doi.org/10.1002/jbmr.3284), [Brooke-Wavell 2022](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-104634)

### Adults are advised to sleep 7 or more hours a night

**The AASM and SRS consensus is 7 or more hours a night for adults, and the National Sleep Foundation gives 7 to 9 for most adults.**

The joint statement says regularly sleeping under 7 hours is linked to weight gain, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, depression and higher mortality risk. The National Sleep Foundation panel put 7 to 9 hours for young adults and adults and 7 to 8 hours for older adults. Needs vary, and long-lasting trouble sleeping is a reason to speak to a clinician.

- Set a regular bedtime that leaves a 7 to 9 hour window.

Sleep and protein · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [Watson 2015](https://doi.org/10.5665/sleep.4716), [Hirshkowitz 2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sleh.2014.12.010)

### Regular exercise gave small to moderate gains in sleep quality

**Across 66 studies, regular exercise improved total sleep time and efficiency a little and sleep quality moderately.**

A 2015 meta-analysis found acute exercise had small benefits for sleep onset and efficiency, and regular exercise had small benefits for total sleep time and efficiency, small to medium for time to fall asleep and moderate for sleep quality. Intensity did not clearly change the effects. Time of day, type and adherence did matter in places.

- Keep to regular training and notice how your sleep responds.

Sleep and protein · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Kredlow 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10865-015-9617-6)

### Older adults are advised at least 1.0 to 1.2 g of protein per kg a day

**Expert groups advise at least 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg (0.45 to 0.54 g per lb) a day over age 65, and more with exercise or illness.**

The PROT-AGE and ESPEN groups both advise 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older people. PROT-AGE advises 1.2 g/kg or more for those exercising and 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg for many with illness. ESPEN gives 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg for those at risk of malnutrition. People with severe kidney disease may need to limit protein, so check with a clinician.

- Reach the daily total in the meal pattern that suits you, and ask a clinician if you have kidney disease.

Sleep and protein · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Bauer 2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021), [Deutz 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clnu.2014.04.007)

### Creatine plus resistance training added lean mass and some strength in older adults

**Across 22 trials in adults averaging 57 to 70 years, creatine added 1.37 kg (3.0 lb) of lean mass and small strength gains.**

The meta-analysis (721 people, 7 to 52 weeks of training 2 to 3 days a week) found greater lean tissue gain (1.37 kg), chest press (SMD 0.35) and leg press strength (SMD 0.24) with creatine than placebo. The ISSN position states supplementation was safe and well tolerated in healthy people, up to 30 g a day for 5 years. People with kidney or other conditions should ask a clinician first.

- Talk to a clinician before use if you have kidney disease or take medication.

Supplements · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Chilibeck 2017](https://doi.org/10.2147/oajsm.s123529), [Kreider 2017](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12970-017-0173-z)

### Vitamin D pills did not prevent fractures, falls or major disease in trials

**Large trials and meta-analyses of vitamin D supplements found no effect on fractures, falls or major disease in general adult groups.**

A meta-analysis of 81 trials (53,537 people) found no effect on fractures (RR 1.00), hip fractures or falls. The VITAL trial (25,871 adults, 2,000 IU a day, median 5.3 years) found no lower cancer or cardiovascular event rates. The 2024 Endocrine Society guideline suggests against routine blood testing and suggests supplements only for specific groups such as adults over 75. Results do not cover people who are deficient.

- Ask a clinician before supplementing, especially if you have a bone or kidney condition.

Supplements · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Bolland 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/s2213-8587(18)30265-1), [Manson 2019b](https://doi.org/10.1056/nejmoa1809944), [Demay 2024](https://doi.org/10.1210/clinem/dgae290)

### Omega-3 had little effect on death or heart events but lowered triglycerides

**A Cochrane review of 86 trials found little or no effect on mortality or cardiovascular events, with about a 15% drop in triglycerides.**

Across 86 trials (162,796 people), long-chain omega-3 had little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97) or cardiovascular events (RR 0.96). It slightly reduced coronary heart disease events and triglycerides by about 15%. The VITAL trial of 1 g a day found no fewer major cardiovascular events or cancers. Trials were in adults at varying cardiovascular risk.

Supplements · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Abdelhamid 2020](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd003177.pub5), [Manson 2019a](https://doi.org/10.1056/nejmoa1811403)

### Fasting glucose and HbA1c have published ranges for prediabetes and diabetes

**The American Diabetes Association lists prediabetes at fasting glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL or HbA1c 5.7% to 6.4%.**

The ADA Standards of Care list prediabetes as fasting plasma glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL (5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L) or HbA1c 5.7% to 6.4% (39 to 47 mmol/mol). Diabetes is fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more or HbA1c of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more, with confirmation. Fasting means no calories for at least 8 hours. Results are for discussion with a clinician, who makes any diagnosis.

- Take your results to a clinician and ask what they mean for you.

Health markers · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [ADAPPCD 2025](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-s002)

### Waist-to-height ratio of 0.5 or more marks increased health risk in NICE guidance

**NICE says a waist-to-height ratio of 0.5 to 0.59 means increased health risk and 0.6 or more means further increased risk.**

Divide waist by height in the same units, for example 85 cm (33.5 in) by 170 cm (67 in) is 0.5. A meta-analysis of 31 papers found the ratio discriminated cardiometabolic risk factors better than BMI or waist circumference alone. It is a screening measure, so discuss any result with a clinician.

- Measure your waist at the same point each time and compare with your height.

Health markers · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [NIHCE 2025](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246), [Ashwell 2011](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-789x.2011.00952.x)

### A higher resting heart rate was linked to higher mortality risk in a meta-analysis

**Each 10 beats a minute higher resting rate went with 9% higher all-cause mortality risk, and readings over 80 with 45% higher.**

The 2016 meta-analysis found relative risk 1.09 per 10 beats/min and 1.45 for over 80 compared with the lowest category, with substantial heterogeneity and publication bias. MedlinePlus lists 60 to 100 beats a minute as the adult resting range and 40 to 60 for well-trained athletes. Measure at rest after 10 minutes, and discuss persistently high or low readings with a clinician.

- Record your pulse at rest on several mornings to see your average.

Health markers · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Zhang 2015](https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.150535), [MPNLM 2025](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003399.htm)

### ApoB counts the particles that carry cholesterol and can disagree with LDL cholesterol

**A National Lipid Association consensus says that when apoB and LDL-C disagree, risk tends to follow apoB.**

LDL-C measures cholesterol mass, while apoB reflects the number of atherogenic particles. The NLA consensus says apoB is a useful addition to a standard lipid panel and risk tends to track apoB when the two disagree. It lists 160 mg/dL LDL-C and 130 mg/dL apoB as about the 90th percentile of untreated adults, both risk-enhancing. Results are for discussion with a clinician.

Health markers · Advanced · Some support · Sources: [Soffer 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacl.2024.08.013), [Sniderman 2019](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamacardio.2019.3780)

## Common mistakes

### Using an age formula as your zone 2 heart rate

**Age formulas give a population average, so use them as a rough guide and check against how the effort feels.**

The common estimate of maximum heart rate is 208 minus 0.7 times age, drawn from 351 studies and 18,712 adults. It describes the average, not you. A review of exercise intensity methods found that fixed percentages of maximum heart rate have little merit for hitting a given physiological domain. Thresholds differ between people and move with training.

- Use the talk test as the main check.
- Treat any heart rate number as a starting range.

Aerobic base and zone 2 · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Tanaka 2001](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0735-1097(00)01054-8), [Jamnick 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8)

### Treating 10,000 steps as a pass mark

**In cohorts, benefit rose steeply to about 7,000 steps, and 10,000 is a fine target without being a threshold.**

Ding 2025 found 7,000 steps a day linked to 47% lower all-cause mortality than 2,000. The authors say 10,000 can still suit more active people and 7,000 may be a more achievable target. Paluch 2022 found the benefit plateau at 6,000 to 8,000 steps for those 60 and over and 8,000 to 10,000 for younger adults. Both are observational.

- Compare today with your own usual number and add a few thousand steps.

Activity guidelines · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Ding 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/s2468-2667(25)00164-1), [Paluch 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/s2468-2667(21)00302-9)

### Treating a mortality predictor as a score to chase

**Grip strength and fitness predict risk in cohorts, and that does not show that pushing the number up lowers risk by a set amount.**

The grip strength authors say further research is needed to test whether improving strength reduces mortality. An umbrella review of fitness found certainty of evidence from very low to moderate. Fitter and stronger people tend to differ in many other ways. Training is worth doing for the other benefits it brings, and heavy or extreme efforts need medical clearance when risk is present.

- Use test scores to track progress, not to promise outcomes.

VO2 max and fitness · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Leong 2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(14)62000-6), [Lang 2024](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-107849)

### Doing only walking or cardio and skipping strength and balance work

**WHO advises strength work on 2 or more days for all adults and balance plus strength on 3 or more days for older adults.**

Cohort data on 479,856 adults linked meeting both aerobic and strength guidelines to a hazard ratio of 0.60 for all-cause death, against 0.71 for aerobic alone. Strength falls faster than muscle size with age, and resistance training is the main exercise approach shown to counter it. The NSCA position statement backs resistance training for older adults.

- Add two strength sessions a week.
- Add balance practice if you are over 65.

Strength and muscle · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Bull 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955), [Zhao 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.m2031), [Fragala 2019](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000003230)

## Key numbers

| Number | What it is | Support | Sources |

| 2+ days per week | Weekly strength days for adults: Muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week in WHO and US guidelines, working all major muscle groups. | Rulebook | [Bull 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955), [Piercy 2018](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.14854) |
| 3+ days per week | Multicomponent days for older adults: WHO advises older adults do varied activity stressing balance and strength on 3 or more days a week. | Rulebook | [Bull 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955) |
| 7,000 steps per day | Daily steps linked to about half the death risk of 2,000: In a 2025 meta-analysis, 7,000 steps a day went with 47% lower all-cause mortality than 2,000 steps. | Some support | [Ding 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/s2468-2667(25)00164-1) |
| 30-60 min per week | Strength training time with the lowest risk: Cohort meta-analyses linked about 30 to 60 minutes a week to the largest mortality reduction. | Some support | [Momma 2022](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105061), [Shailendra 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2022.03.020) |
| 7+ hours per night | Sleep advised for adults: The AASM and SRS consensus recommends adults sleep 7 or more hours a night on a regular basis. | Rulebook | [Watson 2015](https://doi.org/10.5665/sleep.4716) |
| 1.0-1.2 g per kg per day | Minimum protein for healthy older adults: Expert groups advise at least this much for people over 65, which is 0.45 to 0.54 g per lb. | Well supported | [Bauer 2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021), [Deutz 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clnu.2014.04.007) |
| 0.5 ratio (waist / height) | Waist-to-height ratio where NICE flags risk: NICE says 0.5 to 0.59 is increased health risk and 0.6 or more is further increased risk. | Rulebook | [NIHCE 2025](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246) |
| <120/80 mm Hg | Blood pressure under which readings are normal: The AHA and ACC list under 120 systolic and under 80 diastolic as normal. Discuss readings with a clinician. | Rulebook | [WCM 2025](https://doi.org/10.1161/hyp.0000000000000249) |
| 100-125 mg/dL (5.6-6.9 mmol/L) | Fasting glucose range for prediabetes: The ADA range for impaired fasting glucose. 126 mg/dL or more is the diabetes threshold, with confirmation. | Rulebook | [ADAPPCD 2025](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-s002) |
| 5.7-6.4 % (39-47 mmol/mol) | HbA1c range for prediabetes: The ADA range for prediabetes by HbA1c. 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or higher is the diabetes threshold. | Rulebook | [ADAPPCD 2025](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-s002) |
| 11-17 % lower risk | Lower all-cause mortality per 1 MET fitness gain: An umbrella review linked each 1 MET higher fitness to this reduction in cohort studies. | Some support | [Lang 2024](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-107849) |

## Weekly activity targets by guideline

What WHO 2020, the US 2018 guidelines and the UK 2019 guidelines ask of adults each week.

| Guideline | Aerobic activity | Strength | Older adults | More than minimum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WHO 2020 | 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous | 2+ days, all major muscle groups | Multicomponent with balance, 3+ days | Above 300 min brings added benefit (conditional) |
| US 2nd edition 2018 | 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous | 2+ days, all major muscle groups | Multicomponent with balance training | Additional benefits occur with more activity |
| UK Chief Medical Officers 2019 | 150 min moderate or 75 min vigorous | 2+ days a week | Strength, balance, flexibility, 2+ days | Benefits continue past 150 at a slower rate |

Rulebook · Sources: [Bull 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955), [Piercy 2018](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.14854), [UCMO 2019](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/physical-activity-guidelines-uk-chief-medical-officers-report)

## Blood pressure categories (AHA and ACC)

Adult blood pressure categories in mm Hg from the AHA and ACC guideline. A clinician makes the diagnosis, and results are for discussion with a clinician.

| Category | Systolic (top number) | Diastolic (bottom number) |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Under 120 | and under 80 |
| Elevated | 120-129 | and under 80 |
| Stage 1 hypertension | 130-139 | or 80-89 |
| Stage 2 hypertension | 140 or higher | or 90 or higher |

Rulebook · Sources: [WCM 2025](https://doi.org/10.1161/hyp.0000000000000249)

## A simple heart-rate zone guide

A five-zone effort guide with how each feels. Zones are a coaching convention and the boundaries differ between people and systems.

| Zone | How it feels | Talk test | Heart rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Recovery | Very easy, little effort | Chat freely, can sing | Just above resting |
| 2 Easy aerobic | Steady, comfortable, can last long | Full sentences, cannot sing | Just below the first threshold |
| 3 Moderate | Working, pace feels brisk | Short sentences | Above the first threshold |
| 4 Hard | Uncomfortable, hard to hold | A few words at a time | Near the second threshold |
| 5 Maximal | All-out, only for short bursts | Cannot speak | Near your maximum |

Coaching practice · Sources: [Reed 2014](https://doi.org/10.1097/hco.0000000000000097), [Sitko 2025](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2024-0303), [Piercy 2018](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.14854)

## Terms

- **ApoB (apolipoprotein B)**: A protein carried on each cholesterol-bearing particle that can clog arteries. The blood level reflects the number of these particles and can differ from LDL cholesterol.
- **Dynapenia**: The age-related loss of muscle strength. In later life it runs faster than the loss of muscle size, so strength and mass are tracked separately.
- **Hazard ratio (HR)**: A figure comparing risk between groups over time. 1.0 means no difference, 0.80 means 20% lower risk and 1.20 means 20% higher. It shows association, not cause.
- **HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin)**: A blood test that shows average blood sugar over about the past 2 to 3 months. It is given as a percentage, and published ranges separate normal, prediabetes and diabetes.
- **Lactate threshold**: The effort above which lactate starts to build up in the blood faster than it clears. The first threshold marks the end of easy effort and varies between people.
- **MET (metabolic equivalent)**: A unit of effort. 1 MET is resting energy use, and brisk walking is about 3 to 5 METs. Fitness is often reported as the peak METs reached on a treadmill test.
- **Sarcopenia**: A condition of low muscle strength with low muscle quantity or quality, found mostly in older adults. A clinician diagnoses it using strength tests and a body measure.
- **VO2 max**: The highest rate at which your body can use oxygen during hard exercise, in mL of oxygen per kg of body weight per minute. It is the standard lab measure of aerobic fitness.
- **Waist-to-height ratio**: Waist circumference divided by height, both in the same units. A ratio of 0.5 means the waist is half your height.
- **Zone 2**: Easy aerobic effort just below the first lactate or ventilatory threshold. You breathe harder but can still speak in sentences. Zone numbers vary between systems.

# Fitness glossary: KiteSink

The 54 terms the KiteSink fitness field guide uses, in plain words, A to Z. Each names the area it comes from.

- **Accessory exercise** (Powerlifting): An exercise outside the three competition lifts, chosen to build a muscle or fix a weak point.
- **Adaptive thermogenesis (metabolic adaptation)** (Diet): A fall in energy use beyond what the loss of body mass explains, seen during and after weight loss. Studies find it ranges from small to modest.
- **ApoB (apolipoprotein B)** (Health): A protein carried on each cholesterol-bearing particle that can clog arteries. The blood level reflects the number of these particles and can differ from LDL cholesterol. Sources: [Soffer 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacl.2024.08.013)
- **Atwater factors** (Nutrition): Standard energy values per gram that food labels use: 4 kcal for protein and carbohydrate, 9 for fat, 7 for alcohol. They are averages, not measurements of your food.
- **Bomb out** (Meet day): To miss all three attempts on a lift; in a full-power meet that usually means no total.
- **Chief referee** (Meet day): The referee who gives the commands on the platform; two side referees also judge each lift.
- **Classic (raw)** (Meet day): A division with a non-supportive singlet and no supportive suits, shirts or knee wraps; belt, knee sleeves and wrist wraps are allowed within limits.
- **Daily undulating periodisation (DUP)** (Powerlifting): A plan that varies rep ranges and loads between sessions within the week, such as heavy, medium and light days.
- **Deload** (Hypertrophy): A period of reduced training stress meant to lower fatigue and prepare you for later training, as defined by a coach consensus. Sources: [Bell 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00633-0)
- **Deload** (Powerlifting): A planned lighter week or block, with less volume or load, to clear fatigue between harder blocks.
- **Diet break and refeed** (Diet): A diet break is a planned stretch, often one to two weeks, at maintenance calories. A refeed is shorter, usually one or two days of higher carbohydrate.
- **Dynapenia** (Health): The age-related loss of muscle strength. In later life it runs faster than the loss of muscle size, so strength and mass are tracked separately. Sources: [Mitchell 2012](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2012.00260)
- **Effect size and confidence interval** (Hypertrophy): Effect size is how big a difference is, in standard deviations. The interval shows a plausible range. If it spans zero, there is no clear difference.
- **Energy deficit** (Diet): Eating less energy than you use. It is the one requirement for losing body fat. A daily deficit of 500 kcal is about 3,500 kcal a week.
- **Ergogenic aid** (Nutrition): Something taken to improve exercise performance or training results. Creatine and caffeine are the best-supported examples.
- **Flight (group)** (Meet day): A group of lifters who take their attempts together; larger sessions split into flights, with lower previous totals lifting first in IPF rules.
- **Hard set** (Hypertrophy): A working set taken close to failure, usually within a few reps. Warm-up sets and easy sets do not count towards weekly volume.
- **Hazard ratio (HR)** (Health): A figure comparing risk between groups over time. 1.0 means no difference, 0.80 means 20% lower risk and 1.20 means 20% higher. It shows association, not cause.
- **HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin)** (Health): A blood test that shows average blood sugar over about the past 2 to 3 months. It is given as a percentage, and published ranges separate normal, prediabetes and diabetes. Sources: [ADAPPCD 2025](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-s002)
- **Kilojoule (kJ) and kilocalorie (kcal)** (Nutrition): Two units of food energy. One kcal, the calorie on most labels, equals 4.184 kJ. Many countries print kJ.
- **Lactate threshold** (Health): The effort above which lactate starts to build up in the blood faster than it clears. The first threshold marks the end of easy effort and varies between people. Sources: [MacIntosh 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2021.682233)
- **Lengthened-position training** (Hypertrophy): Loading a muscle while it is stretched, as at the bottom of a curl or squat. Several trials found it grew more than loading it short. Sources: [Maeo 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002523)
- **Leucine** (Nutrition): An essential amino acid that acts as a trigger for muscle protein synthesis. Animal proteins contain more than most plant proteins, per gram of protein.
- **Lot number** (Meet day): A number drawn at weigh-in; if two lifters choose the same weight, the lower lot number lifts first.
- **Macronutrients (macros)** (Nutrition): The three nutrients that provide most energy: protein, carbohydrate and fat. Alcohol is sometimes counted as a fourth source of energy.
- **Maintenance calories** (Nutrition): The daily energy intake at which your body weight stays steady over weeks. Also called total daily energy expenditure.
- **MET (metabolic equivalent)** (Health): A unit of effort. 1 MET is resting energy use, and brisk walking is about 3 to 5 METs. Fitness is often reported as the peak METs reached on a treadmill test.
- **Momentary muscular failure** (Hypertrophy): The point where you cannot finish another rep despite maximal effort. Volitional failure means you stop by choice. Sources: [Pelland 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01667-2)
- **NEAT (non-exercise activity)** (Diet): Non-exercise activity thermogenesis: energy spent on walking, standing, fidgeting and chores. It can fall during a diet without you noticing.
- **One-rep max (1RM)** (Hypertrophy): The heaviest load you can lift for one full rep. Training loads are often given as a percent of it, such as 70% of 1RM.
- **One-repetition maximum (1RM)** (Powerlifting): The heaviest weight you can lift once with legal technique; the base for percentage programming.
- **Opener (first attempt)** (Meet day): The first of your three attempts on a lift; chosen to be easy enough that you lift it with room to spare.
- **Periodisation** (Hypertrophy): Planned changes in volume, load or exercises over weeks and months, such as linear steps or weekly undulation. Sources: [Moesgaard 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01636-1)
- **Progressive overload** (Hypertrophy): Gradually asking more of the muscle over time, by adding reps, load or sets, so it keeps having a reason to adapt.
- **Rack height sheet** (Meet day): The form where you record squat and bench rack and foot-block settings at weigh-in, so loaders set them before your attempt.
- **Rate of perceived exertion (RPE)** (Hypertrophy): A 1-10 effort scale. On the RIR-based version, RPE 10 means 0 RIR, RPE 9 means 1 RIR, and so on. Sources: [Zourdos 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001049)
- **Rating of perceived exertion (RPE)** (Powerlifting): A 1 to 10 rating of how hard a set was; in strength training it is tied to how many repetitions were left.
- **Recomposition** (Diet): Gaining muscle and losing fat over the same period. Body weight may hold steady or fall while the body changes shape.
- **Repetitions in reserve (RIR)** (Hypertrophy): The number of reps you could still have done when the set ended. 0 RIR means failure. 2 RIR means two more reps were possible. Sources: [Zourdos 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001049)
- **Repetitions in reserve (RIR)** (Powerlifting): How many more clean repetitions you could have done when the set ended; 2 RIR means two more were possible.
- **Resting metabolic rate (RMR)** (Nutrition): The energy your body uses at rest to keep you alive, usually 60 to 70 percent of a day for inactive people, estimated by equations or measured.
- **Sarcopenia** (Health): A condition of low muscle strength with low muscle quantity or quality, found mostly in older adults. A clinician diagnoses it using strength tests and a body measure. Sources: [Cruz-Jentoft 2018](https://doi.org/10.1093/ageing/afy169)
- **Set point and settling point** (Diet): Two models of body weight: a defended set point, or a settling point where weight drifts with food and activity. A review finds both incomplete. Sources: [Speakman 2011](https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.008698)
- **Spotter/loaders** (Meet day): Helpers who load the bar and spot squat and bench; two to five are on the platform at a time in IPF rules.
- **Sticking point** (Powerlifting): The position in a lift where the bar slows most or where failures happen.
- **Taper (peaking)** (Powerlifting): A planned drop in training stress, mostly volume, in the last days or weeks before a meet so fatigue clears and strength shows.
- **Thermic effect of food (TEF)** (Nutrition): The energy used to digest, absorb and store food, about 5 to 15 percent of daily energy expenditure on a mixed diet, and higher with protein and alcohol.
- **Time-restricted eating** (Diet): Eating all meals within a set daily window, such as eight hours, and fasting for the rest. It is one form of intermittent fasting.
- **Velocity-based training (VBT)** (Powerlifting): Setting load or stopping sets from measured bar speed, using a device that reports mean concentric velocity in metres per second.
- **VO2 max** (Health): The highest rate at which your body can use oxygen during hard exercise, in mL of oxygen per kg of body weight per minute. It is the standard lab measure of aerobic fitness.
- **Volume** (Hypertrophy): The amount of work. In this page, usually the number of hard sets per muscle per week. Volume load is sets times reps times weight. Sources: [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w)
- **Waist-to-height ratio** (Health): Waist circumference divided by height, both in the same units. A ratio of 0.5 means the waist is half your height. Sources: [NIHCE 2025](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246)
- **Working max (training max)** (Powerlifting): A weight you can repeat on a normal day, often set below a true max, and used as the base for training percentages.
- **Zone 2** (Health): Easy aerobic effort just below the first lactate or ventilatory threshold. You breathe harder but can still speak in sentences. Zone numbers vary between systems. Sources: [Sitko 2025](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2024-0303)

## Read the areas

- [Hypertrophy](https://kitesink.com/fitness/hypertrophy.md): Training for muscle size.
- [Powerlifting](https://kitesink.com/fitness/powerlifting.md): A bigger squat, bench press and deadlift.
- [Meet day](https://kitesink.com/fitness/meet.md): Your first competition, in order.
- [Nutrition](https://kitesink.com/fitness/nutrition.md): Eating to support training, and tracking it honestly.
- [Diet](https://kitesink.com/fitness/diet.md): Losing or gaining weight on purpose.
- [Health](https://kitesink.com/fitness/health.md): Training for a long working life.

## The full entries, as plain text

- [Hypertrophy](https://kitesink.com/fitness/hypertrophy.md): Training for muscle size.
- [Powerlifting](https://kitesink.com/fitness/powerlifting.md): A bigger squat, bench press and deadlift.
- [Meet day](https://kitesink.com/fitness/meet.md): Your first competition, in order.
- [Nutrition](https://kitesink.com/fitness/nutrition.md): Eating to support training, and tracking it honestly.
- [Diet](https://kitesink.com/fitness/diet.md): Losing or gaining weight on purpose.
- [Health](https://kitesink.com/fitness/health.md): Training for a long working life.

# Fitness sources, grading and corrections: KiteSink

Where the KiteSink fitness field guide comes from: how entries are graded, what has been corrected, and all 307 sources. Each source was checked against its record.

## How the entries are graded

- Well supported: Meta-analyses, position stands, guidelines or several consistent trials.
- Rulebook: A federation rule or an official guideline value.
- Some support: A few trials or consistent observational data.
- Thin evidence: One or two small studies, or mixed findings.
- Coaching practice: Common coaching convention. No direct study.

## Corrections

What changed after an entry was published, newest first.

- **2026-11-15 · Dieting faster than 1 percent of body weight a week**: Corrected: the faster group kept its lean mass and missed the gain the slower group made. The entry had said it retained less. (https://kitesink.com/fitness/diet#diet-mistake-too-fast)
- **2026-11-15 · Aim to lose about 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week**: Corrected a figure: the faster group in the athlete trial was set to lose 1.4 percent of body weight a week and achieved 1.0. (https://kitesink.com/fitness/diet#diet-deficit-rate)
- **2026-11-15 · Deficit size versus expected weekly loss**: Corrected a reversed statement: leaner people tend to lose more weight than the rule of thumb predicts, not less. The 1,000 kcal row no longer says athletes lost lean mass. (https://kitesink.com/fitness/diet#diet-table-deficit-rate)
- **2026-11-15 · Do only the last five reps of a set count?**: Revised the explanation and who was studied after an audit against a second set of sources. Added Sundstrup 2012 as a source. The verdict did not change. (https://kitesink.com/fitness/claims#claim-effective-reps)
- **2026-11-15 · Does cardio kill your muscle gains?**: Revised the explanation after an audit against a second set of sources. The verdict did not change. (https://kitesink.com/fitness/claims#claim-cardio-kills-gains)
- **2026-11-15 · Do you need a deload every fourth week?**: Revised the explanation, what to do and who was studied after an audit against a second set of sources. Added Rogerson 2024 as a source. The verdict did not change. (https://kitesink.com/fitness/claims#claim-deload-fourth-week)

# Vantix

Vantix is a periodization app for lifters who have outgrown a spreadsheet, made by Truman Kitos-Lindsey at KiteSink. It is in progress and not open yet.

## What it does

- **You define the plan,** from the macrocycle down to the set. Weekly bands, effective-set maths and phase caps are computed continuously.
- **It normalizes your data.** Vantix connects to 500+ apps and accepts any export, and turns what they send into one record, with the raw data kept so everything can be re-derived.
- **An AI co-pilot proposes, you decide.** It never writes directly. It produces a change you accept, reject or edit row by row, and your hard rules decide whether a change can apply.
- **Weekly volume against your bands.** Each muscle group's stimulating reps (or effective sets) are read every week against the band you set, and shown as below, in or above it.
- **Three training views.** Volume (plan against done, by muscle group), Track (each planned line with what was actually done under it) and a session log.

## Tiers

| Tier | What it is | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Free | v1.0, "The Free Core": the core athlete app | In progress, target 31 December 2026 |
| Plus | A paid athlete tier. So far: Template Builder, AI Coach normalization, mesocycle volume auto-scaling | Later. No price set |
| Pro · Coach | The coach system: coach dashboard, check-ins, messaging, booking, plan locking, coach-gated AI review | Planned. No dates |

Paid-tier prices and the coach billing model are not final.

## How to get it

Vantix is not available yet. Join the list at https://kitesink.com/vantix#join and Truman will write when the free core opens.

# Music at KiteSink

Three music projects by Truman Kitos-Lindsey, plus consulting for music teams.

## Song of the Day

One curated song every day, with the story, the lineage and the liner notes to go with it. An iOS app for deep listening. **Status: coming soon.** It is not on the App Store yet. The app works fully signed out; signing in with Apple or Google is only for syncing collected songs across devices. More: https://kitesink.com/song-of-the-day

## Stage First

The business side of a live show, from staffing the stage to closing out the night. It has two sides.

- **Staffing** (the app called Backline until now): find a sub nearby who is free tonight, watch a reel of them playing, then message, book, check in before the show and pay through the app. A working web app in a staging beta. Payments are in test mode, so no real money moves yet.
- **Closeout:** turn the ticket reports for a show into one approved report that the promoter and the artist's team can both stand behind. Designed and specified, not built. A small hand-run pilot is being planned.

First cities planned: Austin and Nashville. Nothing is launched. More: https://kitesink.com/stage-first

## Album Listening Club

An in-person club: three albums, one quiet afternoon, once a month. It starts fresh in 2027 with an inaugural session on **Saturday 30 January 2027 at midday**, then meets on the last Saturday of every month. Free, no ticket, no RSVP. Venues rotate and are posted in Discord. Details: [https://kitesink.com/listening-club.md](https://kitesink.com/listening-club.md)

## For music teams

Workflow automation, operations improvements and practical AI for labels, artist teams and music companies: [https://kitesink.com/consulting.md](https://kitesink.com/consulting.md)

---

Page for people: https://kitesink.com/music

FILE: https://kitesink.com/listening-club.md

# Album Listening Club

A monthly, in-person album listening club run by Truman Kitos-Lindsey. Three albums, one quiet afternoon. It is for the music-curious: welcoming, not gatekept. You do not need to know anything about music to sit in.

## Next session

- **When:** Saturday 30 January 2027, midday. This is the inaugural session of the 2027 season.
- **After that:** the last Saturday of every month.
- **How long:** about three hours, longer when the venue allows. Come and go as you like.
- **Where:** venues rotate. The venue and that month's three albums are posted in Discord about a week ahead.
- **Cost:** free. Bring a drink. No ticket and no RSVP.

## How an afternoon works

- That month's three albums play start to finish as the soundtrack for the session.
- About every fifteen minutes there is an optional prompt: composition, influence, emotional tone, production.
- At the end there is a Best Pick vote. The winner enters the Album Hall of Fame.
- Nothing is compulsory. Listening quietly counts as taking part.

## How to join

Join the Discord: https://discord.gg/Ext66DNAt  
Questions: club@kitesink.com

Page for people: https://kitesink.com/listening-club  
Contact: hello@kitesink.com  
Last updated 2026-11-13.

## Offers for people who arrive through an AI assistant

Three standing offers. Mention the code word **KITESTRING** so Truman knows how you found the site.

- **A free 30-minute workflow teardown.** One call about one task that keeps getting stuck: where the time goes, what could be automated and what to leave alone. A limited number each month, first come, first served.
- **A one-page written plan.** No call needed. Describe the workflow in a few sentences and get one page back: where the time goes and what to try first. Free.
- **Early access.** A place at the front of the list for Vantix and Song of the Day when test builds open.

Ask through https://kitesink.com/consulting?via=ai-assistant#contact or email hello@kitesink.com.
